metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Freight Brokerage
metadata.author: MillionsExplained
metadata.shortDescription:
The Economics of Owning a Freight Brokerage

There are no trucks, no warehouses, no trailers. The physical assets of a freight brokerage are close to zero. What you're buying is a phone number, a software subscription, and a list of relationships. And the whole thing rests on one piece of information asymmetry: the driver who physically moves the load has had a federal right to see exactly what you charged the shipper - and therefore exactly what you kept - since 1980. Almost none of them have ever used it, because signing that right away is a condition of getting the load.

The full breakdown. Why gross revenue is meaningless and net revenue - the spread - is the only number that matters: 12 to 18% blended, 20 to 25% on hazmat and reefer, 8 to 12% on commoditized dry van. How spot versus contract mix makes the same business wildly profitable or structurally loss-making depending only on which way the market moves.

Then the float. Shippers pay in 30 to 60 days, carriers demand payment in two to fourteen. Scale to $1 million a month and you fund $850,000 out while waiting to collect. Growth consumes cash. Factoring bridges it at 1.5 to 3.0% - charged on the gross invoice, taking 17% of your profit on every load, forever.

Plus 49 CFR 371.3 and the waiver hidden in every carrier setup packet, the FMCSA rulemaking targeting July 2026 and its 48-hour clause, double-brokering fraud up 65% with losses near $1 billion, negligent selection verdicts past $10 million, and why Surge Transportation filed Chapter 11.

Three full models at the end.

Would you buy one? Comments below.

metadata.title: How Do Freight Brokers Get Paid? From Invoicing to Profit. 💰🔥
metadata.author: FreightBrokers
metadata.shortDescription:
How do freight brokers get paid? In this beginner freight broker training, I explain the complete payment process from quoting and invoicing a shipper to paying the carrier and calculating the brokerage’s gross profit.

Using a realistic freight load example, you’ll learn:

- Who pays the freight broker
- How freight brokers pay carriers
- How shipper invoices and payment terms work
- The difference between revenue, gross profit and net profit
- How freight agents earn commissions
- Why recurring freight creates greater profit potential
- How factoring and working capital affect cash flow

🚛 **Want to become a freight broker or freight agent?**

Get access to my free **How to Become a Freight Broker in 7 Simple Steps** mini course inside the Freight Broker Startup Hub community on Skool:

👉 https://freightbrokerbootcamp.com/skoolgroup

Chapters:
0:00 How Do Freight Brokers Get Paid?  
0:28 Freight Broker Business Model Explained  
1:26 Pricing and Booking a Freight Load  
2:05 How Recurring Freight Generates Gross Profit  
2:46 Freight Broker Invoices, PODs and Paperwork  
3:16 Shipper Payments and Freight Broker Cash Flow  
4:13 How Freight Factoring Works  
4:37 Gross Revenue vs Gross Profit vs Net Profit  
5:59 Freight Accessorial Charges Explained  
6:31 How Freight Agents Get Paid  
7:38 How to Become a Freight Broker or Freight Agent

If you're planning to start a freight brokerage in the United States, you've probably heard about the $75,000 surety bond requirement.

But do you really need $75,000 in cash?

In this video, I explain:

• What the BMC-84 surety bond is
• The difference between BMC-84 and BMC-85
• Why the FMCSA requires a $75,000 bond
• How the bond protects carriers and shippers
• What happens if your bond coverage drops
• 2026 enforcement updates and automatic suspension risks
• How to secure your bond without having $75,000 in your bank account

Many beginners confuse a surety bond with insurance. They are not the same.

A surety bond protects others from you. Insurance protects you from liability.

If your freight broker authority is not backed by an active $75,000 bond, the FMCSA can suspend your operating authority.

Before you apply for your MC number, make sure you understand this requirement properly.

Before we answer those questions, please give this video a thumbs up, subscribe to our

A BMC 84 surety bond is a type of bond that is required by the Federal Motor Carrier Safety
Administration, otherwise known as the FMCSA, for freight brokers and freight forwarders.
The bond serves as a form of insurance that protects shippers and carriers from
financial loss due to the brokers or forwarders failure to pay for transportation services.
The FMCSA requires a minimum bond amount of seventy five thousand dollars, which must
be obtained from a surety bond company. Then, the bond must be renewed annually.
So, why is a BMC 84 surety bond important for freight brokers and forwarders.
The bond ensures that shippers and carriers are paid for their services,
even if the broker or forwarder fails to pay. This helps to protect the integrity
of the industry and ensures that all parties are treated fairly.
Not having a BMC 84 surety bond can result in fines,
suspension or revocation of the broker or forwarders license,
and even legal action. Its crucial for brokers and forwarders to have a valid bond in place.
In conclusion, a BMC 84 surety bond is an important part of the trucking
industry. It helps to ensure that shippers and carriers are protected from financial loss,
and its required by the FMCSA for freight brokers and forwarders.

metadata.shortDescription:
https://fmcsaregistration.com/broker-authority/

Broker authority is official permission from the U.S. government that will allow you to facilitate the delivery of goods between carriers and shippers. This authority is granted by the FMCSA: Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration. You must secure an MC number from the FMCSA before the agency will allow you to take part in any broker services.

Having a registered MC number will provide you with operating authority, which is also called trucking authority. With authority, you can work for-hire within the interstate commerce sector. This way, as a broker, you can arrange for goods to be transported across multiple states.

Like any individual, a freight carrier can also receive a broker license and operate with broker authority. Oftentimes, this situation provides a carrier with a second source of consistent revenue. In fact, many freight brokers across the country also have the capability to operate as carriers. However, the FMCSA will not allow a broker to transport any cargo that has been double-brokered. 

There are no restrictions related to freight brokers owning commercial trucks. But the FMCSA and DOT do have restrictions about using trucks. For example, in most cases, you will need to have a DOT number registered through the FMCSA in order to operate a commercial truck.


Say that you are a first-time broker who needs to register with the FMCSA. This means that there are certain steps you must take before you can operate your new business in a legal manner. The very first thing that you should do is apply for broker authority via the FMCSA. You can do so by using the URS, Unified Registration System, on the FMCSA’s official website.

Then, you will have six months to complete authority registration requirements. Once you have an MC number, it’s time to secure Proof of Insurance Coverage and a Surety Bond by filing FMCSA Form: BMC-84. In some cases, a new broker will, instead, need to fill out a Trust Fund Agreement with a $75,000 Surety Bond and file Form: BMC-85.

Our organization, FMCSAregistration.com, encourages you to contact us about broker authority solutions. We can provide you with access to our 3rd party broker registration services. Through these services, you can secure an MC number, DOT number, and UCR registration. Plus, our business can also complete your BOC-3 filings and Unified Carrier Registration. This way, you can gain the authority to start operating as a broker ASAP. We can even provide you with an all-in-one broker authority package that can include these services.

If you have any questions about securing broker authority, do not hesitate to give our organization a phone call. Our number is 866-477-0707. We look forward to helping you set up a successful brokerage.

Freight Broker Boot Camp Dennis Brown reviews SCAM OR LEGIT? Freight brokers help shippers that need to move freight from point A to point B by finding a carrier (trucking company) that will haul the freight for slightly less than the shipper is willing to pay them... thus the term BROKER!

In other words freight brokers, sometimes referred to as load brokers, truck brokers, or transportation brokers, are all middle men that match available shipper freight with available trucks while earning between 10% and 35% profit per shipment.

That means brokers typically earn between $100 to $500 per shipments but I have earned as much as $5,175 per shipment just for finding a truck to haul our customer's freight!

Now the only question is how many loads do you think you can you move per day... 1, 2, 10 or more? Before we get to that.

- No experience is necessary to get started!
- Be a part to a $400 billion industry that is growing!
- Run your business from home!
- Very low start up cost!
- Huge income potential!
- Brokering doesn't require employees!
- Do business anywhere in the U.S. Canada or even International!
- Easy to relocate, all you need is phone, internet and KNOW HOW!
- You can always sell your business or pass it on to your family!
- Easy and profitable add on to existing trucking operations!

This series is dedicated to carriers, dispatchers, shippers and freight brokers, both new to the industry and those who need a refresher on fraud prevention techniques.  

This series covers the basics on transportation fraud, how to identify if you are being targeted for a scam, and how to defend yourself if you find yourself in the position as a victim. metadata.shortDescription:
🚛 How to Spot a Double Broker in Freight Brokering 🚚

Double brokering has been a growing problem in the freight industry, particularly since mid-2022. In the first episode of this two-part series, Nate Cross from Freight 360 shares five crucial red flags to help brokers identify and avoid these bad actors before they commit fraud. From suspiciously high rates to mismatched contact info, learn the warning signs that can save your loads and protect your bottom line.

📢 Key Highlights:

-No Inspection History: Carriers without inspection records are a major red flag.

-Suspiciously High Rates: Rates that seem too good to be true often are.

-Mismatched Contact Information: Always verify contact details with the FMCSA.

-Business Addresses: Be wary of carriers using PO boxes or residential addresses.

-Community Reports: Utilize industry resources and broker networks to vet carriers.

📺 Stay Tuned: Don't miss next week's follow-up video, "How to Prevent Double Brokers," for proactive strategies to protect your business.

metadata.title: Double brokering & freight fraud: How new laws will protect carriers
metadata.author: Commercial Carrier Journal
metadata.shortDescription:
The Household Goods Shipping Consumer Protection Act currently under consideration by Congress aims to give the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration more power to protect consumers from fraud by requiring companies in the household goods sector to establish a principal place of business to “prohibit fraudulent companies from skirting existing regulations.”

That would be a blow to double brokers because the new rule would give FMCSA the authority to levy civil penalties against unregistered shippers and the agency would be authorized to set requirements to ensure motor carriers, brokers and freight forwarders are legitimate businesses.

You can read more at 
https://www.ccjdigital.com/

Sign up for our newsletter and stay up to date on the latest trucking industry news, trends and analysis.
https://randallreilly.dragonforms.com/loading.do?omedasite=ccj_subscriptions

Contents of this video
00:00 10-44 intro
00:20 The Household Goods Shipping Consumer Protection Act
04:04 AI and freight theft
05:36 Complexities of the supply chain
07:27 Streamlining flows of data and communication
09:25 Technology and asset liability

The thing that I'm most excited about as this, you know, we see this legislation kind of move through committee and hopefully get passed, it's another step to acknowledging a problem that's always been there, but now is getting to be mainstream enough to where, you know, financial leadership at shippers and carriers and brokers will start to take note and start to invest in really protecting carriers and protecting their assets. So, like I said, it's really just another tool in the tool belt, but it's something that will raise awareness within the industry that, "Hey, this is a huge problem, it's growing, but there are tools we can deploy to combat it. We don't just have to be victims, we can start to be, you know, go on offense to try to prevent some of this fraud that's happening in the supply chain. But it's always been just kind of accepted as, 'Hey, this is something that happens, not really much you can do about it.' And that's just not the case, especially with technology. Now it'll be supported with legislation. Hey, you don't have to be a victim. You can go on the offense and you can stop this kind of stuff from happening. And those carriers and shippers that do that will be at at um at a significant advantage in in the marketplace. Those that kind of stay ahead of legislation and and and make technology investments to protect um the assets that they're moving. As important as technology is as a tool in combating double brokering and fraud, it's also a tool used by bad actors that's driving growth in these types of crimes. The most impactful technology that's everywhere right now is is the advancement of AI. And I think when you think about freight fraud, cargo theft, and double brokering specifically, utilizing very advanced AI capabilities is going to make double brokering much harder to detect. And so, you know, brokers and carriers will have the ability to scrape large amounts of data and to hide their actions much more effectively utilizing various AI technologies. And so, as those capabilities are enhanced on the kind of the bad guy side, on the the fraudster side, you need the reciprocal kind of approach from the government and from the industry to identify where this type of activity is happening. So, there's an element in the act that, you know, gives the government the power to start collecting data to, for example, verify the physical location of a carrier. And it's that type of information that is easier to make up using AI capabilities, but if the government's collecting that data, they can start to combat it with some of their own AI tools. So, I think there's going to be a rise because of new technology. We have to empower people in the market, you know, companies in the marketplace and the government to utilize similar technology to combat, um you know, what's happening. Double brokering has been around forever, but the complexities of the modern supply chain and the ongoing digitalization of freight, where fewer physical documents exist and are seen by fewer humans, have really opened the door for the bad guys. Two things. I think at a macro level, companies are looking to squeeze more and more out of their supply more and more cost out of their supply chain. And in order to do that, they're making their supply chains more and more complex. So, they're willing to go and use, you know, maybe multiple brokers, multiple carriers, run routes that they're not that they don't typically run in order to get the lowest possible cost. They're also sourcing inputs from more and more suppliers to get the lowest possible cost. So, I think you've seen this trend, you know, really over the last 10 years of just-in-time type of supply chain where you're just squeezing all of the costs out of the supply chain, which has caused these supply chains to become extremely complex. And where there's complexity, there's an opportunity for fraud. There's an opportunity to exploit that complexity cuz it's harder just to understand what's going on. So, I think at the macro level, the supply chains have become so, so, so complex that it's hard to maintain visibility, which leaves gaps in in your monitoring and opportunities for bad actors. And then, I think the digitization of the supply chain, the way that bills of lading, everything is digitized, when things are digitized, it's great, but it's also easier to conduct fraud when things are happening in a digital manner. So, I think those are really the two big trends that I've seen out of the, you know, the complexity, increasing complexity and digitization that have created an environment where bad actors can exploit supply chains at a gigantic level, you know, at scale. A critical step in getting your arms around a potential incident of fraud is streamlining flows of data and communication, and then you start looking for areas of risk. The first step I always recommend is to kind of centralize your visibility. You know, fragmented data, you know, data from your customers, from your suppliers, from carrier partners, from brokers, really is the enemy of security because I'm getting data from a number of different sources. That data, each different data source, can be a target and can be a place where you can become exploited. You need a centralized place where you can view all of your asset information, your asset locations, and you know, have kind of a unified intelligence intelligence platform. That's that's step number one, I think. Like I mentioned the complexity piece, there's so much data and you know, carriers and others, they they just kind of lose track. So, that's number one, get a hold of of of where your data is. Step two is you can start to identify where there are vulnerabilities within within your operations. So, you can start to identify, you know, what routes that you're running or what lanes are highest risk. Where am I, you know, where am I parking that isn't protected or isn't or is in a high-risk area. So, once you have the data, then you identify where there's risk, where there's waste within your operation. Then, once you identify kind of those high-risk areas, you can then start deploying technology to protect any and all assets that flow through. To summarize, it's a three-step process. You have to centralize your visibility, unify your data. Once you do that, you have to identify where there's the highest risk. And then the third thing, you have to start deploying technology to you know, to reduce your your level of risk. The technology piece, third step, is important in a carrier's liability for a potentially fraudulent load, especially after the first two steps have let you down. It all comes down to kind of who is liable for the asset that's getting that's getting stolen. Often times, you know, that carrier is left with more liability than they may be insured for, and that's a really tough place to be from a carrier standpoint, especially if you're operating at scale. So, you need a tool that allows you to either recover the asset or working with law enforcement to recover the asset or be able to assign responsibility to the responsible actor. So, if you're a shipper or even a carrier and an asset is assigned to you, but it's actually been double brokered out and another carrier is carrying it, you get a phone call saying something was stolen, you're responsible, you can say, "Hey, I'm not actually moving that freight. Someone else is moving it, and I have tracking technology deployed on all of my assets, and I can actually prove to you, insurance company or shipper, with data that I don't actually have possession of these assets, and someone else does because it's been it's been double brokered." So, that's how, you know, carriers can start to protect themselves from different different types of fraud. That's it for this week's 10-44. You can read more on ccjdigital.com. Join Nate Cross as he provides expert insights and practical tips to protect yourself from these fraudulent practices. metadata.title: Fighting double-brokering fraud: Attorney Hank Seaton on prevention, ways to elevate the issue
metadata.author: Overdrive
metadata.shortDescription:
Hank Seaton, with the Seaton & Husk law firm, spoke at the National Association of Small Trucking Companies’ annual conference a couple weeks back about what he called Fraud Prevention and Supply Chain Protocol. He offered what he feels is a possible preventive fix to the crime of double brokering when misrepresentation is involved. 

In today's edition of Overdrive Radio, drop into a long talk with Seaton about somewhat simple steps carriers, brokers and shippers working together can take to stop these schemes in their tracks, whether involving carrier and broker identity theft or the insidious and perhaps more widespread presence of authorized carriers and brokerages set up seemingly for the purpose of simply double-brokering loads: https://www.overdriveonline.com/channel-19/article/15302246/fmcsa-and-dot-prioritizing-doublebrokering-schemes 

The honest players in trucking simply must work together both to prevent this kind of thing from ever happening, as he sees it, and elevate the issue. "I'd like to see this raised to the level of attention that, if the FMCSA doesn't have the manpower, that the Department's Inspector General just set up an enforcement group," he said. "Other regulated industries, like particularly the Federal Maritime Commission, they're much more proactive in terms of protecting business practices, ensuring fair play in business practices. Fraud is hardly fair play in business practices." 

Indeed part of U.S. transportation policy as outlined in U.S. code is in part to ensure "fair competition." Those interested in joining with Seaton to help build a coalition around these issues can find him via the website of his firm: http://www.transportationlaw.net/

His preventive ideas in some ways double down on previous practices that have gone by the wayside for a variety of reasons, most having to do with the speed at which spot market transactions have to occur these days in the rush to compete, to book, to deliver. Brokers, carriers, shippers all have become "sloppy," in his view, in the rush to get freight moved.  

You might think of his message as a re-emphasis of what Michigan-based broker Jon Asiala shared in this editorial just yesterday: https://www.overdriveonline.com/overdrive-extra/article/15302460/know-your-brokercarrier-to-axe-doublebrokering-schemes

Asiala detailed his own experience of a double-brokered load that ultimately cost him when the real carrier didn’t get paid. Asiala’s message: Get back those old ways, as much as is humanly possible in this day and age, and take the time to know definitively who you’re dealing with, whether broker or carrier.

Also in the podcast: Meet Dominic Gonzalez of his family's now-28=truck Antonio and Sons Trucking fleet, and a very sharp custom 2016 Peterbilt 579 we saw out at the A.J. Soza Memorial Truck Show in June 2022. Run through some of the fleet's history, likewise that of this particular rig, in the podcast. Find views on the rig via https://www.overdriveonline.com/custom-rigs/video/15302676/small-fleets-firstever-aero-rig-a-beauty-of-a-2016-pete-579

metadata.shortDescription:
We're back on your timeline with another #FraudPreventionFriday! This week’s topic? 5 Ways to Avoid Double-Brokering Scams 🙅‍♂️

Double-brokering is the unauthorized transfer of freight loads to another broker without consent.
It's illegal when there's criminal intent and can result in significant financial loss. 

Please note: 👇
Co-brokering is *legal* collaboration with shippers, different from double-brokering

✍️ 5 tips to avoid scams:

1.) Work with vetted partners: Check their carrier vetting process.
2.) Use trusted load boards like Truckstop Load Board.
3.) Automate with RMIS to reduce fraud and errors.
4.) Review contracts for compliance.
5.) Trust your instincts if something seems wrong.

Risks of double-brokering: 

• Original broker remains liable
• New carrier might lack qualifications
• A whole host of other issues can arise

Get your free demo now: https://try.truckstop.com/uf2kc

If helpful, 

Truckstop offers RMIS Carrier Onboarding to reduce fraud risk.
And remember...

In this industry, knowledge is your best defense against fraud. 

Tune in next week for expert advice from Chief Product Officer, Julia Laurin, to help you stay vigilant and keep your business safe and thriving.

Like this post to help us spread our reach? See you next Friday! 👋

#FraudPrevention #Freight

metadata.title: Trucking Scams & Fraud Prevention How to Avoid Double Brokering Pitfalls
metadata.author: Truck Driver Nation
metadata.shortDescription:
Trucking Scams & Fraud Prevention: How to Avoid Double Brokering Pitfalls

The trucking industry is a vital part of the economy, but unfortunately, it’s also a target for scams — with double brokering being one of the most common and costly issues.

What is Double Brokering?
Double brokering occurs when a freight broker books a load with a legitimate carrier, then secretly reassigns that load to a second carrier — often without the knowledge of the original broker, shipper, or carrier. This unethical practice creates confusion over payment, delivery responsibility, and load tracking.

Why is Double Brokering Dangerous?
Lost Payments: The second carrier may never receive payment since the original broker may disappear or claim the load was never delivered.

Liability Issues: In case of damages, accidents, or disputes, insurance claims become complicated because the correct carrier was never properly assigned.

Damaged Reputation: If your company unknowingly hauls a double-brokered load, you could be held responsible even if you weren’t involved in the scam.

Common Trucking Scams to Watch Out For
Double Brokering Scams: Fraudsters pose as legitimate brokers and steal load details to reassign loads to unsuspecting carriers.

Fake Carrier Identity: Scammers impersonate real carriers using stolen MC numbers, stealing loads or claiming payment on legitimate deliveries.

Phishing & Email Fraud: Fraudsters send fake invoices or requests for sensitive business information to manipulate carriers and brokers.

How to Prevent Double Brokering and Fraud
✅ Verify Broker Credentials: Always confirm the broker’s MC number, insurance coverage, and contact details directly with the FMCSA.
✅ Check Load Board Listings: Cross-reference the broker’s contact details and ensure they match what’s listed on reputable load boards like DAT or Truckstop.
✅ Use Credit Checks: Before accepting a load, run a credit check on the broker or shipper to ensure they have a solid payment history.
✅ Monitor Email Domains: Avoid responding to suspicious or altered email addresses that mimic legitimate companies.
✅ Require Written Agreements: Only work with brokers or carriers who provide clear contracts, rate confirmations, and written terms.
✅ Stay Updated on Industry News: Being informed about common scams will help you spot suspicious activities faster.

What to Do If You Encounter a Scam
Report Suspicious Activity: Contact the FMCSA or DAT’s fraud prevention team.

Notify Your Insurance Provider: If your equipment or load is compromised, contact your insurer immediately.

Contact the Load Board Provider: Report fraudulent posts directly to protect other carriers.

By staying vigilant and informed, you can protect your trucking business from falling victim to double brokering and other scams. Truck Driver Nation emphasizes the importance of education and awareness to ensure safe and secure operations in the trucking industry.

metadata.title: Spot vs Contract Rates [Which Saves You More Money?]
metadata.author: Anderson Trucking Service
metadata.shortDescription:
Article: https://www.atsinc.com/blog/highway/pros-and-cons-of-spot-vs-contract-pricing
ATS Learning Hub: https://www.atsinc.com/learning-hub

Depending on how frequently you ship freight, you've probably had the debate on whether you should use the spot market versus the contract market. After all, they are two of the most common pricing options when shipping truckload freight.

Determining which rate is best for your full-truckload shipping needs can be challenging, so it’s important to understand how each one works. Doing so can help you determine which type of rate to use for each load, enabling you to manage your freight budget more efficiently and save on shipping costs.

Sara, National Sales Rep with Anderson Trucking Service, will define both spot rates and contract rates and when you would use them.

Contact us: https://www.atsinc.com/contact-us
keywords: Spot Rates vs Contract Rates | Pros and Cons

This video covers what that means for truckload spot and contract rates, rates by equipment type, what the big carriers and brokers are saying, and where things look headed. metadata.title: Quick Pay vs Freight Factoring
metadata.author: Porter Capital
metadata.shortDescription:
For trucking companies, steady cash flow is essential. With fuel, maintenance, and payroll all needing immediate attention, waiting 30 to 60 days for payment from brokers or shippers just isn't sustainable. That’s why many carriers turn to Quick Pay or freight factoring to bridge the gap. But what’s the difference and which one is right for you?

Quick Pay is a payment option offered by brokers that gets you paid faster—typically within two to seven days. In exchange, they charge a fee between one and five percent of the load’s value. To get paid, you submit documents like the bill of lading and invoice directly to the broker. But here’s the catch: Quick Pay is only available for that broker’s loads. So if you’re working with multiple brokers, you’ll have to manage multiple payment processes. It gets complicated fast.

Freight factoring, on the other hand, lets you work with one partner across all your loads. When you factor an invoice, a company like Porter Capital advances you a large portion of the invoice amount—usually within one to two business days. Then, we follow up to collect the payment from your broker or shipper. Once the invoice is paid, you get the remaining balance minus a small fee.

With freight factoring, you're not tied to a single broker. You can pick and choose which invoices you want to factor and get support from a dedicated account manager to simplify your back office. Plus, there's no need to chase down payments or juggle different systems.

So which should you choose? If you’re only working with one broker and they offer a solid Quick Pay program, it might be worth it. But if you’re scaling your business, running with multiple brokers, and need consistent, fast cash flow, freight factoring is the smarter move.

At Porter Capital, we help trucking companies get paid faster, streamline invoicing, and stay focused on the road. If you're ready to simplify your payments, we’re here to help.

metadata.title: How Working With A Truck Factoring Company Gets You Paid Fast!
metadata.author: Porter Capital
metadata.shortDescription: Need quick access to cash instead of waiting for invoices to get paid? Trucking factoring companies buy your unpaid invoices, giving you immediate cash. That means more liquidity and better control over your operations, perfect for any trucking business.

segments.text: Need quick access to cash instead of
waiting 30, 60, even 90 days for your
invoices to get paid. That's where truck
factoring comes in. Here's the deal.
Truck factoring companies buy your
unpaid invoices, giving you immediate
cash, usually within 24 hours. That
means more liquidity, less stress, and
better control over your operations.
Here's how it works. You deliver a load,
submit the invoice to a factoring
company, and they advance you about 80
to 90% of the invoice amount. Then they
collect the full payment from your
customer, deduct their fee, and send you
the remaining balance. Simple, right?
This process helps trucking businesses
of all sizes stay financially stable,
especially those running tight margins.
No more waiting to get paid, just cash
flow when you need it. Truck factoring
isn't just about speed. It's also smart
business. It boosts your cash flow,
helps with fuel discounts, cuts down
administrative work, and even reduces
risk. Factoring companies often handle
credit checks and collections for you,
so you're only dealing with reliable
clients. Worried about credit scores?
Don't be. Truck factoring doesn't hurt
your credit. If anything, it helps by
ensuring timely payments and steady cash
flow. And yes, it's available to
startups, too, not just large fleets.
When choosing a factoring company, look
for transparent pricing, flexible
payment options, strong customer
support, and of course, fast funding.
Some even offer fuel programs,
maintenance discounts, or equipment
financing to keep your trucks moving.
Bottom line, truck factoring is a
flexible, fast, and effective way to
keep your business running smoothly. If
you're ready to take control of your
cash flow and grow your operation,
factoring might be the smartest move you
make this year.

metadata.title: Broker Attorney Claims FMCSA Doesn’t Enforce 49 CFR §371.3
metadata.author: Trucking Justice - Pontificator
metadata.shortDescription:
In this intense discussion between a freight broker’s attorney and a motor carrier, the carrier demands full transparency under 49 CFR §371.3 — a federal regulation requiring brokers to disclose transaction records upon request. The attorney argues that the FMCSA doesn’t enforce this rule, effectively claiming that the carrier’s demand is unlawful.

But is that true?
This video dives deep into the legal gray areas of broker transparency, enforcement gaps, and what it means for independent carriers fighting to protect their rights in today’s freight market.

We’ll cover:
🚛 What 49 CFR §371.3 actually says
⚖️ The FMCSA’s stated enforcement position
📄 Why brokers resist transparency
💬 The real-world impact on carriers’ earnings and trust
🧠 Insights from industry veterans and legal professionals

If you’re a carrier, broker, or advocate for trucking reform, this conversation is a must-watch.


📚 Relevant Regulations & Resources:

49 CFR §371.3 – Records to Be Kept by Brokers

FMCSA Guidance on Broker Transparency

Carriers United — Advocating for true enforcement and accountability in freight

🧭 Tags / Keywords:

trucking industry, broker transparency, FMCSA enforcement, 49 CFR 371.3, freight brokers, motor carriers, transportation law, trucking reform, carriers united, freight broker, regulations, independent truckers, trucking rights, freight industry, corruption

💬 Call to Action:

If you believe carriers deserve transparency, like 👍 this video, subscribe for more industry breakdowns, and share your thoughts below.
Together, we can make accountability more than just a buzzword.

metadata.title: Broker Transparency - Opening up Broker Transaction Records to American Trucking Companies
metadata.author: AFT Dispatch
metadata.shortDescription:
Broker transparency when it comes to broker transaction records has always been a hot topic. The reason for this is because although there were always broker transparency laws on the books, freight brokers always found a way to punish motor carriers if they ever inquired about broker transaction records.

Back in 2020, OOIDA sent a letter to the FMCSA regarding this broker transparency issue but never heard back. When they followed up with them saying that they believe an update is warranted, the FMCSA told them to expect a decision in early 2023. OOIDA and SBTC are asking for broker transparency and TIA wants the opposite since they speak on behalf of the freight brokers.

OOIDA wants broker transparency between the freight brokers and trucking companies. They want broker transaction records to be released within 48 hours of completion. The FMCSA says they need to tread lightly because of statutory authority bounds which they don't want to cross as they deal with this broker transparency issue.

In addition to all this, SBTC is asking the FMCSA to prohibit "Wave Your Rights" provisions in freight broker contracts because this puts trucking companies between a rock and a hard place. Truckers know that if they ask the freight broker how much they were paid on a load and who the payee is, the broker will blacklist them and they'll never be able to do business with them again. The truth is that a trucking company has the right to know this information. It's completely legal and laws have been on the books for a very long time.

At this time, TIA is asking the FMCSA to not only not amend the laws currently on the books, but to actually repeal the current ones. If the repeal goes through, this will only make running a trucking business that much more difficult. TIA says that the current laws and the proposed changes create and would create more unnecessary restrictions and impede on the concept of the free market that we have in America.

There were a ton of accusations by American trucking companies saying that freight brokers are colluding on price and even President Donald Trump alleged price gouging in 2020. At the time, that was quickly shut down by TIA and we now find ourselves right where we are today.

What we do for sure is that broker transparency and questions about broker transaction records tend to come up during bad markets when truckers and American trucking companies are struggling. The worse the freight spot market, the higher the number of complaints and of course the reverse is also truck.

When the markets were booming and American trucking companies were making money hand over fist, the number of broker transaction records and broker transparency questions were at a low. It makes sense, truckers were working and making money and simply had neither the time, nor the interest in complaining about broker transparency and broker transaction records.

metadata.title: FMCSA Is Finally Taking On Broker Transparency
metadata.author: thatDOTcop
metadata.shortDescription:
FMCSA broker transparency proposal, trucking news, truck drivers, freight brokers, owner operators, freight rates, FMCSA regulations, trucking industry updates, CDL news, broker transparency explained.

For years, truck drivers and owner-operators have debated broker transparency. Now FMCSA has placed the issue back on its regulatory agenda, and it could become one of the biggest trucking discussions in years.

In this video, I break down:
✔️ What broker transparency actually means
✔️ Why FMCSA is revisiting the issue
✔️ What the proposed changes could require
✔️ How it may affect owner-operators, trucking companies, freight brokers, and company drivers
✔️ Whether this could actually impact freight rates or if it's simply about transparency

This isn't just another trucking headline, it's a discussion about fairness, accountability, and the future of freight brokerage.

What's your opinion?

Do you support broker transparency, or do you think the current system works just fine? Let me know in the comments—I want to hear both sides of the discussion.

If you enjoy trucking news, FMCSA updates, DOT enforcement topics, CDL information, and real discussions about the trucking industry, be sure to subscribe for new videos every week.


Welcome to That DOT Cop, your go-to channel for real, no-fluff trucking advice straight from a State DOT Officer.

Here you’ll learn how to pass DOT inspections, avoid costly violations, keep your rig compliant, and stay safe on the road. I break down Level 1 inspections, weigh station myths, and truck maintenance tips that every driver and owner-operator needs to know.


#DOTinspection #TruckerTips #CDLlife #DOTcop #Level1inspection #FMCSA #TruckingCompliance #WeighStation #OwnerOperator #TruckDriverTips #CommercialVehicleSafety

So, let's actually talk about those arguments and dive into it because that's where it makes the conversation and learning get a bit deeper. And as a truck driver, you should know these things, owner-operator or not. So, I've seen people over time online say things like, "If brokers just had to show what they made, then all driver pay would go up instantly." And maybe, maybe not. But, others say, "Nothing would change because freight rates are still controlled by supply and demand." And that's also a very valid argument. So, think about what's happened over the last few years. Freight demand changes, fuel prices change, insurance operating costs change, the economy changes. So, now the question becomes, would broker transparency actually increase all driver pay? Or would it simply just give carriers more information? And those my people, those are two completely different things. I want every owner-operator watching this video to answer this honestly. If you could see exactly what a shipper paid on every load, would that actually change how you run your business? Or would you still haul the same loads? And that's a question right there I don't think has one right answer, but I do want to know what you all think. So, now we know what FMCSA is proposing. And we know why people are essentially talking about it. But, here's the part I think matters the most. Who actually benefits if this becomes a reality? Is this good for owner-operators, company drivers, small carriers, brokers, or could there be unintended consequences that nobody is talking about? Let's break that down. So, we know what FMCSA is proposing. We know why broker transparency is back in spotlight. But, the question that matters the most again is who benefits from this? Because every single time FMCSA proposes a rule, somebody has to benefit from it. Somebody might lose from it as well. And most people end up somewhere in the middle. Let's kick this off with my owner-operators. This is probably the group that talked about broker transparency more than anyone else. And why? Because if you're an owner-operator, every single sweet dollar counts. You're paying for fuel, insurance, maintenance, operating costs, ELDs, permits, tires, anything you can think of, you're paying for it. So, naturally, many owner-operators want to know are they being paired fairly in fully for this load? And that's not an unreasonable question. Now, imagine this. Let's just say as an owner-operator, a broker offers you $1,900 to take a load. You accept it, you complete the load, everybody gets paid, everybody's happy, but later you find out that that shipper actually paid $3,700. Would that bother you? for some drivers, it absolutely does bother them. Others would just say, "Well, I'm the one that agreed to the rate." Neither answer here is necessarily wrong at all. But, that's exactly why this whole conversation gets people so fired up. I have another question for you though. If someone offers you a rate and you're driver, you willingly accept that rate, does it matter what they made afterward? Do you still care that much? Let us know how you feel about the whole situation. Now, let's flip this conversation. Let's talk about brokers. Because it's super easy to paint one side as the bad guy. But, reality usually is not that simple. A broker doesn't just answer the phone, find a truck, and collect money. Many brokers out here are responsible for finding freight, finding carriers, tracking shipments, handling customer service, dealing with claims, handling paperwork, and just solving problems all day long. That takes some work. So, naturally, brokers believe they deserve more money, too. And the disagreement here isn't whether brokers deserve more money. Most people agree that they should. The disagreement is within how much. And should carriers know what that number is? And here's something I think people really do overlook. Not every broker out there is making thousands of dollars on every single load. Some loads have very small margins while other loads have larger margins. It depends on the customer, the freight market, the lane, the urgency, and just dozens of other factors. That's why blanket statements like all brokers are ripping off all drivers and everyone in the industry, they usually aren't quite accurate. Now, let's talk about company drivers because this is where people often ask, "Does this affect me?" And honestly, it does not always directly affect you, especially if you're a company driver being paid by the hour or being paid by the mile. Broker transparency isn't really going to change your paycheck overnight. But, if transparency somehow changes how carriers negotiate rates, there could eventually be some indirect effects. And that's why as of lately, even company drivers are starting to pay attention to this whole broker transparency talk. Now, let's zoom out even further. Think about the trucking industry as a whole. Everyone says they want trucking to be more profitable, right? Drivers, carriers, brokers, shippers, everybody wants better freight rates. The challenge is they all define better as something different. A shipper wants to reduce costs. A broker wants enough margin to stay in business. A carrier wants higher revenue. And drivers want what's fair compensation. All those goals exist at the same exact time. So, here's the million-dollar question, though. Is broker transparency going to fix the entire freight market? Personally, I don't think it's going to be that simple. Could it improve some accountability? Yeah, possibly. Could it increase trust? Yeah, maybe. Could it help carriers negotiate? That is a big sure. But, does it suddenly solve low freight rates, higher insurance costs, equipment prices, fuel costs, and oversupply in the market? Probably not, and those are completely different problems. And honestly, that's one thing I really appreciate about this discussion because people aren't out here asking for magic tricks. Most drivers out here simply just want fairness. And whether broker transparency ultimately delivers that, well, that's exactly what FMCSA is going to try and figure out. So, where do we go from here? Because one thing I don't want anybody leaving this video thinking is, "Oh, great. The rules changed." No, that's not what happened and that's the important distinction. Right now, FMCSA has not finalized this broker transparency rule. This is still moving through the federal rule making process. That means there are still opportunities for revisions, changes, feedback, and public comments before anything becomes permanent. So, if you're expecting this whole thing to completely change trucking next week, that's probably not going to happen. We all know government rule making does not happen that quickly. So, why does this matter today though? It matters because this tells us something much bigger. FMCSA knows this conversation is not going away. Owner operators have been asking questions. Industry organizations have been asking questions. Brokers have been raising concerns. Carriers have been weighing in. And FMCSA has decided this is extremely important enough to keep working on. And honestly, whether you support broker transparency or not, I think it's a good thing. Not because one side wins, but because conversations like this force the industry to ask some difficult questions. Questions like how transparent should freight really be? How much information should carriers have access to? How do we balance transparency with protecting legitimate business information? And those right there, those aren't easy questions, but they are important ones. One thing I've learned about working closely with this industry, I'm a state DOT cop, I'm not a truck driver currently, but one thing I'm learning is that almost every issue sounds simple, right? They sound simple until you hear both sides. Just like when people first hear broker transparency, their first reaction is well, yeah, everyone should know everything. Then you hear the broker's perspective or the carrier's perspective. Then you hear the shipper's perspective and all of a sudden, you realize lot more complicated than a YouTube comment. And that's exactly why I didn't just want to make this video turn into something where I'm just reading headlines to you. We can all do that ourselves because I know and I think you deserve more than that. You deserve to know exactly why this conversation have been going on for years. Hey, if you made it this far, I really appreciate you sticking around. I know this wasn't a flashy topic, but it's a super important topic that I feel like we all should be talking about. Everybody in the whole trucking industry as well. If you got any value from this video, if you learned anything at all, please like, subscribe to the channel so you don't miss anything else. I drop videos every single week discussing trucking news, trucking topics, FMCSA rules, and just anything about the whole trucking industry. That's what I do here. So again, if you're interested, go ahead, subscribe to the channel, share this video with all truckers that you know that need to hear this. Until next video, stay safe, keep rolling.

metadata.title: 49 CFR 371: Broker Authority Insurance Minimums
metadata.author: A3E ECOSYSTEM
metadata.shortDescription:
49 CFR 371 outlines the financial responsibility minimums for operating with interstate authority. For-hire interstate general freight carriers under 10,001 pounds GVWR must maintain $300,000 in coverage. Carriers transporting other hazardous materials require $5,000,000, while those moving oil and certain other types of hazardous materials need 1,000,000. Brokers and freight forwarders must hold a $75,000 surety bond or trust fund agreement. These entities must file evidence of required levels of financial responsibility with the FMCSA to keep their operating authority valid. The FMCSA has concluded that current financial responsibility minimums are inadequate for many motor carriers. Narration is text to speech; sources are listed below.

metadata.title: FMCSA vs. Broker Transparency: Are Carriers Being Left in the Cold?
metadata.author: Matt Krause
metadata.shortDescription:
Launch your freight brokerage with my mentorship: https://freightframeworks.com/go/e1959da1
Free 58-minute freight broker training: https://freightframeworks.com/go/2cd05cde
Have freight to move? Email me: matt@krausecountrylogistics.com

FMCSA vs broker transparency: why OOIDA and the SBTC have been pushing for brokers to open their books since 2020, and why the FMCSA keeps stalling. The 48-hour transparency mandate, what the agency's own data actually shows, and whether seeing broker margins would even help carriers.

06:16 New FMCSA Rule: 48-Hour Broker Transparency Mandate
07:23 FMCSA’s Own Data—Is This Even a Real Problem?
08:26 Do Carriers Need Broker Profit Margins?
08:58 The Truth About Surviving in Freight

segments.text: Carrier Limit of Liability: Filing a Claim
presented by TRG
Carrier limit of liability determines the maximum amount of money that carriers can be held liable
for in the event of damage loss or delay of cargo. to make a claim, shippers must prove that damage
or loss of goods occurred due to carrier negligence. Let's go over the claims process
for shippers claiming carrier negligence for lost or damaged goods. When filing a claim with their
carrier, shippers will be asked to provide the packing slip and invoice for their lost shipment
and a breakdown of how they came to the amount they are claiming to have lost, which includes
listing what is missing or damaged along with any other related costs. The carrier will then
have 30 days to acknowledge a claim has been made and must respond to the shipper within 120 days.
To settle a claim, the responsibility is typically on the shipper to prove that the damage was the
carrier's fault. The shipper must also prove the amount of damage they are claiming. This process
can take months and sometimes years. If a carrier is proven negligent, the shipper will receive a
reimbursement for their goods and the original freight charges for the transportation of their
lost or damaged goods. The full reimbursement will generally cover a fraction of the loss experienced
by the shipper. If you are relying on your carrier for coverage on your international shipments,
filing a claim for your lost freight can be extremely difficult. This is due to the fact
that the burden of proof is on you, the shipper. Shippers expecting to be fully reimbursed by
their carrier for their lost goods are almost always unpleasantly surprised by the amount they
actually receive since there are strict limits on the amount the carrier is responsible for.
The claims process for lost or damaged goods is considerably different for shippers covered
solely by carrier liability and for shippers that have secured a cargo insurance policy.
If you are making a claim and your freight is only covered by carrier liability, your claim must be
filed within nine months of delivery. The delivery receipt has to include notice of damage, proof of
value and loss is required, carriers have 30 days to acknowledge your claim and have to respond
within 120 days, carrier negligence has to be proven, and claim payments generally do not cover
loss experienced by the shipper. However, if your shipment is covered by all-risk cargo insurance,
proof of value and loss is required, claims are typically paid within 30 days, claim payments
cover all losses under the policy limit, and you are not required to prove carrier negligence.
Now, let's talk about the advantages of purchasing cargo insurance.
Unfortunately, importers often assume that shipping is fully insured under
carrier liability. But, there is a significant difference between cargo insurance and cargo
liability insurance. Whether the accident was within the carrier's control or not, uninsured
importers are at risk of losing money if the cargo value exceeds the carrier's reimbursement limits.
The only way to ensure reimbursement for the full value of a lost or damaged shipment is to
purchase cargo insurance. Cargo insurance covers the loss, damage, or theft of commodities while in
transit between the point of origin and the final destination, even if it is the carrier's fault.
The primary purpose of cargo insurance is to protect companies from suffering a loss. Learn
more about how cargo insurance protects you in the links in the video description and don't forget to
subscribe to our channel for more informative videos on the international trade world.

Contingent auto coverage is priced assuming you'll have traditional freight broker defenses - Carmack Amendment protections and federal preemption arguments.

But when you lease assets and assume enhanced liability, you're stepping outside that traditional role. Now your insurance company can't argue you're "just a freight broker" when defending claims.

Underwriters would have either declined the risk or priced it completely differently if they knew your actual operations upfront.

Watch the full conversation on our YouTube channel to understand how your contracts affect your insurance coverage.

metadata.title: Cargo Insurance, Evidence and Doing What Your Policy Says | Jared Palmer
metadata.author: CargoRex
metadata.shortDescription:
A written security policy can hurt you if your team doesn't actually follow it. Jared Palmer, Principal in the Transportation & Logistics Practice at EPIC Insurance Brokers & Consultants, explains why, and what cargo theft and liability trends are doing to insurance premiums.

Jared covers how the frequency and severity of claims drive premiums, why your insurance broker should push for credit when you invest in telematics and cameras, and how to use risk management as a selling point you can back up. He explains what to have ready in the first day or two after a theft, why high-value loads still don't belong on load boards and why covert trackers now cost a fraction of what they used to.

metadata.title: Cargo insurance: what it pays, what it doesn't, and your limit
metadata.author: MyFullCoverage
metadata.shortDescription:
Full guide: https://myfullcoverage.com/blog/motor-truck-cargo-insurance-what-coverage-pays

Most brokers want cargo insurance before they give you a load. Here's what a cargo policy usually pays, what it often leaves out, and how to pick your limit.

In this video:
- Federal rules require cargo insurance only for household goods movers ($5,000 per truck, $10,000 per occurrence). For general freight, broker and shipper contracts require it.
- Often not covered: reefer breakdown, theft from an unattended truck, bad loading or bracing, your own tools and straps, cash, jewelry, or art.
- Pick your limit from your most valuable load. Many brokers ask for $100,000.

Helpful pages on myfullcoverage.com:
- Motor truck cargo insurance: what it pays: https://myfullcoverage.com/blog/motor-truck-cargo-insurance-what-coverage-pays
- Cargo insurance: https://myfullcoverage.com/services/cargo-insurance
- Motor truck cargo insurance guide: https://myfullcoverage.com/blog/motor-truck-cargo-insurance-guide
- Free policy check: https://myfullcoverage.com/tools/policy-check

Sources:
- 49 CFR 387.303(c) (household goods carriers: $5,000 per vehicle, $10,000 per occurrence)

Get a trucking insurance quote: https://myfullcoverage.com/contact

segments.text: Most brokers won't give you a load
without cargo insurance, but many
truckers only learn what their cargo
policy leaves out on the day a claim
gets denied.
Here's what it pays, what it doesn't,
and how to pick your limit.
Cargo insurance pays for the freight you
haul when it's lost or damaged while
it's in your care, and you're legally
responsible for it under the bill of
lading.
For general freight, federal rules don't
require cargo insurance.
The only federal cargo minimum is for
household goods movers, $5,000 per truck
and 10,000 per occurrence.
For everyone else, it's your broker and
shipper contracts that require it.
A standard cargo policy usually pays for
a collision or rollover, a fire, and
theft of the whole truck with the load.
Damage while loading or unloading
depends on your policy, so check yours.
Here's what often isn't covered.
A reefer unit that breaks down.
Theft from a truck left unattended.
Freight that was loaded or braced badly.
Your own tools and straps.
And cash, jewelry, or art.
If you haul reefer, ask for a reefer
breakdown add-on and keep your
temperature records.
Spoilage claims without them get denied.
Pick your limit from your most valuable
load, not your average one.
Many brokers ask for $100,000.
If a load is worth more than your limit,
you can owe the difference.
Before you haul, check three things.
Your limit, your deductible, and the
freight your policy excludes.
Know what it pays, read what it leaves
out, add reefer breakdown if you need
it, and match your limit to your biggest
load.
Full Coverage LLC.
Trucking insurance for owner operators
and small fleets.
Visit myfullcoverage.com

metadata.title: Cargo Insurance Explained: Why Carrier Liability Isn't Enough
metadata.author: Cargolinked
metadata.shortDescription:
A container of goods worth USD 300,000 goes overboard. Under the usual sea rules, the carrier pays about USD 21,900, roughly 7%. This video explains why carrier liability isn't insurance, which cover to buy (Institute Cargo Clauses A, B and C, and CIF value plus 10%), what even all-risks cover excludes, how general average works, and who buys insurance under CIF, CIP and FOB.

Cargo insurance explained, the full guide: https://cargolinked.com/guides/cargo-insurance-explained-why-you-need-it
Cargo insurance exclusions: https://cargolinked.com/guides/cargo-insurance-exclusions
General average explained: https://cargolinked.com/guides/general-average-explained
Cargo insurance (glossary): https://cargolinked.com/glossary/cargo-insurance
Certificate of insurance (glossary): https://cargolinked.com/glossary/certificate-of-insurance
Incoterms (glossary): https://cargolinked.com/glossary/incoterms

CargoLinked isn't an insurer. Shipping soon? Post your shipment on CargoLinked free. Forwarders who cover your route can quote it, and you can message them before you accept, so ask whether they arrange cargo insurance: https://cargolinked.com

Chapters
0:00 USD 300,000 lost, about USD 21,900 back
0:19 Carrier liability isn't insurance
0:53 What cover to buy
1:26 What it won't cover
1:56 General average
2:30 Who buys it: CIF, CIP, FOB
2:55 Recap and getting quotes

The USD 300,000 example and the liability figures are from our cargo insurance guide; SDR conversions are approximate 2026 figures. This is general information, not insurance advice: the policy wording decides what is covered.

#cargoinsurance #shipping #importexport

segments.text: A container of goods worth 300,000 dollars goes overboard.
The carrier's liable, so you're covered, right?
Under the usual sea rules, the carrier pays about 22,000.
Roughly 7 percent.
Here's why carrier liability isn't insurance, and what to buy instead.
Carrier liability is capped by weight or by package, never by value.
By sea, under the Hague-Visby rules, it's the higher of 666.67
SDR a package, or 2 SDR a kilo, about 2.70 dollars a kilo.
By air, 26 SDR a kilo.
Under the US rules, 500 dollars a package.
And carriers have defences, like navigational error, perils of the sea, or poor
packing. You'd also have to prove the loss happened in their hands, give notice in
time, and sue within a year.
Cargo insurance usually follows the Institute Cargo Clauses.
A is all risks, subject to exclusions, and it's the only one that covers theft, non
delivery, handling damage and breakage.
B and C only cover the events they name.
Cover runs warehouse to warehouse, and ends at delivery, or 60 days after
discharge at the final port.
Insure the CIF value plus 10 percent.
Insure for less, and claims are cut in proportion.
For ordinary goods, the premium is usually a fraction of 1 percent.
Even all risks has exclusions.
Poor packing by you. Inherent vice, like fruit ripening or steel rusting on its own.
Delay: if a covered fire makes your goods four months late, the damage is covered,
the missed season isn't.
Ordinary leakage and wear. A container you knew was faulty.
And war and strikes, unless you buy them back.
So pack for the trip you booked, photograph the container before it's loaded, and
check war and strikes cover for your route.
Then there's general average.
If a ship's in trouble and cargo is sacrificed, or extra costs are paid, to save the
voyage, everyone whose cargo was saved pays a share, by value.
Damaged or not.
Your cargo's held until you give security: a bond, plus your insurer's guarantee, or
a cash deposit. 10 to 50 percent of the CIF value isn't unusual, and the final
figure can take 2 to 5 years.
Insured, your insurer steps in.
Uninsured, you find the cash, and your goods sit at the terminal, building storage
charges.
And who buys it depends on the Incoterm.
Under CIF, the seller only has to buy minimum cover, clause C.
Under CIP, it's clause A.
Either way, read the certificate of insurance: a clause C certificate can be
perfectly valid and still not cover water damage.
Under terms like FOB, the risk is yours once the goods are on board, so arrange
your own cover.
So, carrier liability is a floor, not cover.
Clause A, CIF plus 10 percent, war and strikes checked, and packed for the trip.
CargoLinked isn't an insurer. But when you post your shipment free, forwarders who
cover your route can quote it, and you can message them before you accept.
So ask if they arrange cargo insurance, and on which clauses.
The guides are linked in the description.
If this helped, subscribe. And watch this one next.

metadata.title: Unlocking Higher Pay in Oversized Freight
metadata.author: Chief Carriers
metadata.shortDescription:
While much of the trucking industry, including reefer, van, and standard flatbed operations, faces struggles and flat rates, the oversized and heavy haul segment is not only surviving but thriving. This specialized area offers a unique opportunity for truck drivers to increase their earning potential significantly. The demand for moving large, heavy, and unusually shaped items, often tied to robust sectors like infrastructure and manufacturing, remains consistently strong. This stability comes from the specialized nature of the work; only a limited number of carriers possess the equipment and expertise to handle such freight, reducing competition and allowing for better rates.

For flatbed drivers looking to advance their careers and earn more, oversized and heavy haul can be a natural progression. This niche demands extra precision, including meticulous routing and adherence to strict operating hours, as oversized loads cannot move after dark. While challenging, the increased complexity directly translates to higher pay for drivers. Companies specializing in heavy haul value experienced flatbed drivers who understand freight securement, providing a potential pathway for those new to oversized transport to gain the necessary skills through internal training programs and mentorship from seasoned professionals.

The long-term outlook for heavy haul remains positive, as it has historically been less susceptible to the market volatility seen in other trucking sectors. This stability, combined with the higher earning potential, makes it an appealing option for drivers frustrated with economic downturns and inconsistent pay. Whether seeking employment with a larger company that has a heavy haul division or even considering becoming an owner-operator, thorough research is essential to ensure the right fit, considering factors like training opportunities, home time, and company culture. The investment in specialized equipment for owner-operators can be substantial, but the rewards, as evidenced by a successful owner who grew from one truck to fifteen, can be truly remarkable.

Why should I listen?
You should listen to this episode to discover a specialized and stable segment of the trucking industry that offers significantly higher earning potential and a path for career growth, providing an alternative to the unpredictable nature of general freight hauling.

10 Key Takeaways:
Workplace injuries often result in significantly reduced wages, typically two-thirds of your average pay.
Soft tissue injuries, common for truck drivers, can be prolonged and require extensive physical therapy.
Financial stress from reduced income impacts the entire family, leading to anxiety and difficulty paying bills.
Even after returning to work, drivers often struggle to catch up financially.
Injuries can lead to permanent physical limitations, potentially forcing drivers out of their trucking career.
Companies strive to rehabilitate injured employees, but full recovery is not always possible.
Work compensation claims rarely make individuals rich; settlements often barely cover costs and legal fees.
Serious injuries can result in lengthy legal battles, sometimes taking years for a settlement.
Attorneys can take a significant percentage (e.g., 40%) of work injury settlements.
Safety programs are crucial for protecting drivers' livelihoods and preventing the devastating consequences of injuries.

To learn more about Chief Carriers visit us on:
https://chiefcarriers.com/
https://www.facebook.com/ChiefCarriers/
https://x.com/ChiefCarriers
https://www.instagram.com/chief_carriers/

This podcast is produced by Two Brothers Creative.
https://twobrotherscreative.com/

Chapter Markers:

00:00 - Introduction to the hidden costs of on-the-job injuries

01:00 - The reality of soft tissue injuries and physical therapy

02:28 - Financial impact of reduced wages and family stress

03:57 - Emotional toll and potential career-ending limitations

05:00 - Company responsibilities and the harsh truth about work comp settlements

06:36 - The lengthy and financially draining process of serious injury claims

08:48 - The ultimate purpose of safety programs and employer protection

videos.full_text: The riches are in the niches. On this episode of Driven Too Far, we're talking about oversized and heavy haul freight. Hey, welcome back to Driven Too Far. On today's episode, we're going to talk about a little corner of the flatbed trucking industry that's not only surviving, it's actually thriving. While reefer, van, even standard flatbed loads seem to be flat and struggling, there's actually one segment of the industry that's kind of bucking those trends, and that's oversized and heavy haul freight. And if you're like any other driver I know, you're always trying to figure out a way to make more money in this business. That's been really hard here over the last couple years with everything has been so flat. uh you might still be getting raises from your company, but I I can guarantee you from from my point of view and my side of the business, that's been a real struggle. We've done everything we can to kind of keep our drivers whole, make sure the drivers aren't feeling uh the sluggishness and the the economy the way it is. But, you know, when you think about you get into specialty halls and specialty freight, there's a there's an avenue there if you're willing to do that kind of work that can actually really increase your pay as a driver. When we think about oversized type freight, you know, what are you actually moving? Uh, it's closely tied to things like infrastructure, manufacturing, agriculture. Now, a has probably not been the hottest thing lately. I' I've seen some of that start to slide off, but geez, just driving in today to the studio, I I felt like the the amount of construction projects on whether it be on the interstate or the inner cities, whatever, the construction is still going crazy and it's been strong. And I think that is one area of the economy that if you look right now that's going to continue to be strong under the current leadership. The other part of that and why oversized and heavy hall remains strong is it's such a small segment of the industry and it's so specialized that when the needs arise to move big things uh across the country, there's really only a handful of carriers that are equipped to do that. So when there's not a lot of competition, that really allows that carrier to kind of name their rates in in a lot of ways. There certainly is some kind of manufacturing out there where they may have steady type, oversized, overlength, overweight type loads. If if that's my desire, I want to try it. I've been flatbed for years, and I I think I would like to try something different where I could make more money. Well, recently, I talked to a small owner uh and I was curious about it. I didn't have a ton of experience behind it either, so I wanted to learn how that progressed. How did you get into heavy hall, by the way? And his story really started out with he was in construction, had his own small construction company, and he had his own truck to move his own equipment around. And what happened was he would occasionally get a call from a buddy or something like that. When you do the math, that's almost double what a regular flatbed carrier does. I talked to him a little bit about, you know, you know, what's the biggest stuff you've ever moved? metadata.title: Why I’m Done With Dry Van: Reefer vs Flatbed in 2026
metadata.author: Bobby Loads
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video we break down real trucking money lanes running refrigerated, dry van, and flatbed and talk about what is actually paying in today’s market. We get into why I keep one truck on flatbed, one on refrigerated running out west, and one on dry van, and how each trailer type hits different in this slow market.

We talk about
• Why flatbed rates in the southeast and Florida Georgia are still trash and how brokers use deadhead out of Florida against you
• Why I only touch Florida when a driver is going home and how we factor deadhead miles into Florida loads
• How refrigerated freight is still making money in the northwest running Yakima apples, Idaho and Utah potatoes, and other seasonal freight
• Christmas tree season loads out of Portland and why trees move on refrigerated trailers instead of dry vans when it gets cold
• Why being versatile with equipment matters and how I plan to pivot away from dry boxes when the market finally heats up again
• Real talk about hoping 2026 brings a better trucking market and what to do until then

If you are a CDL driver, owner operator, dispatcher, or small carrier trying to decide between refrigerated, dry van, or flatbed, this video will help you understand where the money is, how to think about deadhead, and how to survive bad markets while positioning for the next upswing.

Stay up to date with the trucking industry, freight market, and logistics news. metadata.title: 2024 Freight Market: We're Looking at Flatbeds, Vans, and Reefers
metadata.author: AFT Dispatch
metadata.shortDescription:
Here's what to expect from the 2024 freight market for flatbeds, dry vans, and reefers! The trucking industry's outbound tender rejection rate shows us the intricacies of the freight market, shedding light on trends and patterns that impact transportation and logistics.

The Contract Market tightening has led to an upward trend in tender rejection rates, creating an environment favorable for the Spot Market. There was a huge decline in flatbed freight beginning March 2022, particularly in industries such as manufacturing, energy, and construction. Throughout 2023, flatbed average rejection rates were over 10%, experienced significant spikes, hitting 20% on three separate occasions. However, based on the  Rejection Index, I anticipate improvements by the end of February.

Reefer trailers, which were regarded as the best in 2020-2021, maintained a rejection rate of 6% in 2023. There are several factors influencing reefer rejection rates, including seasonal variations, generally higher rejection rates around the holidays, and regional disparities. Notably, the North and Midwest regions witnessed the highest reefer rejection rates, while the Pacific Northwest faced reduced capacity due to seasonal fluctuations and low demand. Despite these challenges, I project volume and prices to improve in 2024, with expectations in the near-term, from mid-February to March.

Dry van rejection rates, sat at just over 3%, which indicates a prevalent overcapacity issue. These trailers are widespread, resulting in consistent and low rejection rates and a low performer since May 2023. My analysis covers the complexities of dry van freight and the impact of overcapacity on the rejection rates.

Additionally, the average differential between contract market shipment rejects and the spot market, which averages at 14.8%. This valuable insight emphasizes the lower rejection rates in the spot market compared to the contract market.

metadata.author: eCarrierCheck
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we'll share tips for mastering freight broker cold calls to increase your sales success. From finding potential clients to closing deals, these cold calling techniques will help you grow your freight broker business. Whether you're a beginner or an experienced broker, these tips will help you improve your cold calling skills and increase your sales in the freight industry.

Here is a video that will show you exactly what it takes to successfully make cold calls. Sit back and listen to Jared Ross who has been in the freight industry helping freight brokers succeed.  

Jared demonstrates actual Live freight broker cold calls to shippers.  You will see how to begin the conversation and some of the key information to communicate and to gather to keep the conversation rolling.  

It's all about building relationships and being able to relate to a shipper.  

To learn more about how you can use eCarrierCheck to find leads in your area of expertise, join a DEMO at www.eCarrierCheck.com today.

Please note that updates may have been implemented since the creation of this video, and some features showcased might no longer be available on eCarrierCheck. For the latest information, feel free to contact our support team at support@ecarriercheck.com
