https://freightbrokerbootcamp.com/nobrokers - I was turned away by a shipper who says, “We don’t use freight brokers”? In this video, I share the freight broker sales response that turned one hard NO into a long term customer worth over $100,000 in gross profit. Including a free word for word freight broker sales script you can download below.

Learn how to use this freight broker cold calling script when a shipper says, “We don’t use brokers.”

In this video, I explain the exact objection handling response I used to turn a cold call rejection into a test load and eventually more than $100,000 in gross profit. 

You’ll learn how to overcome shipper objections, differentiate your brokerage and earn the opportunity to quote freight without sounding pushy.

👉 Download my FREE “We Don’t Use Brokers” sales script
https://freightbrokerbootcamp.com/nobrokers

👉 Join the FREE Freight Broker Startup Hub community
https://freightbrokerbootcamp.com/skoolgroup

👉 GET TRAINED as a freight broker or freight agent 100% risk free at https://FreightBrokerBootcamp.com

Chapters:
00:00 Freight Broker Objection: “We Don’t Use Brokers”
00:48 Why Shippers Refuse to Use Freight Brokers
01:37 What to Say When a Shipper Says No
02:29 How Freight Brokers Build Trust With Shippers
03:39 Ask the Shipper for One Test Load
04:15 Freight Broker Follow-Up for Repeat Loads
04:54 How One Cold Call Generated $100,000
05:19 Freight Broker Objection-Handling Strategy
05:43 When a Shipper’s No Really Means No
06:07 Free Freight Broker Cold-Calling Script

#freightbrokerbootcamp #freightbrokertraining #freightagenttraining #freightbrokersales

segments.text: She said, "We don't use brokers." And
then turned into over $100,000 in
profit. Let me tell you a quick story.
It all started when a prospect said, "We
don't use brokers." And I said, "Good.
I'm glad to hear it." She was a bit
confused and then said, "Why are you
glad? I just told you no." That
conversation started as a cold call
rejection, but within 2 weeks, she gave
me a test load. That load generated
about $150 in profit, but eventually
became a customer worth over $100,000 in
gross profit. Today, I'm going to show
you exactly what I said, why it worked,
and how you can use the same basic
approach when a shipper tells you, "We
don't use brokers." But the first thing
I had to understand was what her
objection really meant. Because
sometimes no really does mean no. And
sometimes it's just an escape button.
This prospect worked for a pet food
company. It wasn't a referral. It wasn't
a warm lead. I picked up the phone and
cold called them. When she said she
didn't use brokers, I could have thanked
her and ended the call. That's what most
brokers do, right? And that was exactly
what she wanted. You see, another broker
had burned her in the past. So, whenever
a freight broker called, she said, "We
don't use brokers." The broker usually
hung up and she could go back to work.
That line had become her escape button.
Now, sometimes a company genuinely has a
policy against brokers. It's rare, but
it does happen. If that's the case,
respect it and move on. That wasn't the
situation here. Her company could use
brokers. She just didn't trust them. And
honestly, after what had happened, I
couldn't blame her. So, I didn't need to
convince her that all brokers were
great. I only needed enough time to show
her that we might be different.
When she gave me the objection, I said,
"Good. I'm glad to hear it." Then, I
stopped talking. That wasn't the
response she expected. She was used to
brokers thanking her and just hanging
up. Instead, I said something that made
her curious enough to ask, "Why are you
glad?" Now, I wasn't trying to be
clever. I was just trying to break the
pattern long enough to keep the
conversation alive. Then I said, "Oddly
enough, several of my customers said the
exact same thing when I first contacted
them." Then I asked, "Do you want to
know why they eventually decided to work
with us?" She said, "Yeah, why?" Okay,
so now for a second, think about what
just happened. A few seconds earlier,
she was trying to end the call. It was a
hard no. Now she's asking me to explain
why we were different. That hard no
became a real conversation. But getting
her attention wasn't enough. I still had
to overcome the reason she didn't trust
brokers.
I explained that one of the biggest
differences was accountability. A lot of
brokers are easy to reach when they're
trying to get your freight, but what
happens after 5:00? What happens on
weekends? And what happens when a driver
has a problem and the shipment is
suddenly in trouble? That's when some
brokers cut and run. And I told her
that's where I shine because I make
myself accessible to my clients. If
something went wrong, I wasn't going to
disappear or pass the buck. But just
telling her wasn't enough. Every broker
says, you know, they provide great
service. So, I shared a real customer
story. A driver hauling a customer
shipment experienced a major health
issue. We had to recover the freight,
arrange for a transload on the fly, and
get the shipment on another truck.
Despite everything that happened, the
load still delivered on time. That story
showed her what I meant by
accountability. Then, I showed her
something she probably wasn't expecting.
I had a testimonial from that exact
customer praising us for being
accessible, responsive, and accountable
during the emergency. I didn't just make
a claim. I gave her a real example and
then I backed it up with proof directly
from the customer. That gave her a
reason to believe we might actually be
different. But I still didn't ask her
for all her freight.
I asked her for just one opportunity,
one test load. That's it. She didn't
have to replace her existing carriers or
brokers. She didn't have to give us
every lane. She didn't have to make
long-term commitments. She could test us
once and judge us based upon what
actually happened. Within about two
weeks of the first call, she gave us a
shipment. That load generated about
$1,500 in revenue and maybe about $150
in gross profit. It picked up, it
delivered, and everything went smoothly.
We did exactly what we promised, but
getting the test load wasn't the big
lesson in this story. What happened
after I delivered was what turned into a
long-term customer. After the load
delivered, I followed up. I didn't
assume she was happy just because
everything looked good on my end. I
asked and she confirmed that she was
satisfied with the service. Now, this is
where many brokers could say, "Great.
Give me a call if you need anything."
Then they'd hang up and wait. I didn't
do that. I asked, "When's the next load
on that lane shipping?" She told me it
was going the following week. So, I
asked for it and she gave it to me on
the spot. That became another
opportunity to prove ourselves. Then
came another load and another and
another. A successful Tesla doesn't
always automatically create repeat
business. You still have to follow up
and ask for the next opportunity.
That first load generated about $150 in
profit, but eventually turned into about
$20,000 a year in profit. And the
relationship lasted for over five years.
Altogether, a cold call that started
with we don't use brokers produced over
$100,000 in gross profit. And none of it
would have happened if I had treated her
first objection as the end of the
conversation.
So the next time a shipper says, "We
don't use brokers," don't argue or hang
up. Find out whether it's a company
policy or whether another broker burned
them. If it's a bad experience, explain
one meaningful way you're different.
Prove it with real customer story or
testimonial and ask for one opportunity
to prove yourself. Not all of their
freight, just one test load. Then
deliver, follow up, and ask for the next
one.
Now, I'm going to keep it real. Not
every shipper who says we don't use
brokers will become a customer.
Sometimes no really does mean no. But
don't automatically assume the first
objection is the real objection. In this
case, one quick response earned a few
more seconds. Those seconds created a
conversation and that conversation
earned one test load and that $150
profit load eventually became $100,000
in gross profit. So, let me know in the
comments based on everything I just
shared with you. How confident are you
in handling the we don't use brokers
objection on a scale of 1 to 10? Again,
hit me up in the comments. And to make
this easier, I put together a free word
for word we don't use broker script you
can keep beside you when you're
prospecting. Use the link in the
description to download the free copy.
And while you're there, make sure you
join my new freight broker startup hub
community on school where you can
connect with other aspiring and new
brokers. Again, both links are in the
description. I'll see you in the next

segments.text: So, the reason most freight brokers fail
on cold calls isn't the script. It's
because they don't know how to handle
objections. Every shipper has them. And
if you freeze, the call ends before it
even begins. So, in this video, I'm
going to show you exactly how to handle
the three most common objections every
shipper will throw at you and then how
to flip them into opportunities and the
exact responses that keep the
conversation alive. So, if you want to
explode your sales, you must first
understand why shippers give you
objections in the first place. Most
freight brokers are taught to be
enthusiastic and pitch their services
and overcome objections with like clever
rebuttals. When a shipper says, "We're
happy," the broker says, "Hey, but we
can we can save you money." According to
behavioral science and sales experts,
this approach is fundamentally flawed.
When you tell people things, when you
attempt to dominate or push them, you
are the least persuasive. When you call
a shipper sounding excited, aggressive,
or needy, like what we call commission
breath, you trigger their brain into
fight orflight mode. Okay? They don't
see you as a solution. They see you as a
typical salesperson trying to force
something on them. The objection is
their flight response. An attempt
basically to get you off the phone as
quickly as possible. To succeed, you
must stop being a product pusher. Okay?
Basically pushing rates and trucks and
become a problem finder. We use a
methodology called NEPQ, which is
neuroeotional persuasion questioning.
This isn't about manipulation. It's
about changing your communication style
to lower sales resistance and allow the
prospect to persuade themselves. And the
key is detachment. You need to sound
neutral and calm and genuinely unsure if
you can even help them yet. And this is
the fastest way to disarm a prospect.
So, let's break down the three biggest
objections and how to handle them.

metadata.shortDescription:
If you are a dispatch agent, load planner or another member of the operations team, you’ve come to the right place! In this training, we will review load building, load management, dispatching, handling documents, managing drivers & assets and Ascend’s amazing AscendPortal and more!

Looking to find shippers, get shipper leads, and grow your freight brokerage without the headache?

AscendTMS has you covered! Whether you’re figuring out how to start a freight brokerage, become a freight broker, manage one, or simply need to find direct shippers, our free (and best) TMS software makes it easy.

With freight broker tools, shipper lists, and logistics TMS software built for success, we help you research shippers, land shippers, manage loads, streamline operations, grow your freight brokerage, and make some real money in the freight brokerage world.

Stop searching where to find shippers or how to manage your loads and your freight —and start booking loads today with AscendTMS, the #1 freight broker TMS!

Learn more and GET YOUR FREE TMS at: https://www.thefreetms.com

metadata.title: How to Get Paid Detention, Layover & Accessorial Pay as a Truck Driver
metadata.author: Think Trucking
metadata.shortDescription:
How truck drivers get paid for detention, layover, and accessorial time — instead of waiting for free at shippers and receivers. This video covers what detention pay is, when it kicks in, how to document your time, and how to ask for layover and accessorial pay so it actually shows up on your settlement.

Gear links below are affiliate links — as an Amazon Associate I earn from qualifying purchases.

In this episode of Trucking Business Explained: what detention pay is (2 hours free, then $30–$75/hr), what layover pay covers ($100–$175/day after 24 hours idle), and the full accessorial menu — truck-ordered-not-used, lumper fees, tarping, extra stops. Plus the national numbers: detention costs for-hire truckload drivers $1.1–$1.3 billion a year (DOT Inspector General, 2018), and a 15-minute increase in dwell time raises crash risk 6.2%. We close with the exact 5-step checklist drivers use to actually collect it.

00:00 Detention Pay: Six Hours at a Dock, Nobody Paid
00:34 What Detention Pay Actually Is for Truck Drivers
01:23 Detention Pay Math: 4 Billable Hours at $60/hr
02:03 Layover Pay: Waiting Between Loads
02:42 Accessorial Pay: TONU, Lumper Fees and Extra Stops
03:50 Detention Costs Truck Drivers $1.1–$1.3 Billion Every Year
04:25 Detention Safety Crisis: +6.2% Crash Risk
05:22 Why Detention and Layover Pay Keep Going Unpaid
06:23 How to Collect Detention Pay: 5-Step Checklist
07:48 Company Drivers: Detention Pay Pass-Through Question
09:45 Detention, Layover and Accessorial Pay Checklist

Nobody paid him for a single one of
them.
>> That is not a rare horror story.
That is a normal Tuesday in American
trucking, and the money he was owed has
a name.
>> Today on Trucking Business Explained, we
break down detention pay, layover pay,
and accessorial pay. What they are, the
rates, and the exact steps drivers use
to actually collect them.
>> Because here is the uncomfortable truth
about this money.
In most cases, it exists.
It is in the contract. And drivers still
do not get it.
>> Let us start with detention pay.
Detention is compensation for the time
you spend stuck at a shipper or receiver
beyond the agreed window.
You are parked, you are not moving, and
the clock is running on your 14-hour
day.
>> The industry standard is two free hours.
The first two hours at the facility are
on the house.
Paid time starts after hour three, and
only if you know how to claim it.
>> Typical detention rates run $30 to $75
an hour, paid in half-hour or hourly
increments.
Some specialized freight pays more, but
30 to 75 is the standard band in the
published guides.
>> Here is the first trap. That 2-hour
grace period is measured from your
appointment time, not from when you
actually arrive.
Show up early and sit for an hour before
your appointment, and that hour may not
count at all.
>> Now, let us do the illustrative math.
You wait 6 hours total.
Two are free. That leaves four billable
hours at, say, $60 an hour.
That is $240 you are owed.
does not sound like life-changing money
until you realize that is roughly what a
driver earns driving 3 to 400 miles. It
is half a day of driving spent sitting
still.
>> And it compounds.
Lose 3 hours past free time twice in 1
week at $60 an hour, and that is $360
gone.
Do that every week and you have given
away a truck payment every single month.
>> Now layover pay, which is different.
Layover covers the time between loads.
You delivered, you are empty and
available and dispatch has nothing for
you.
You are stuck, sometimes for days.
>> Layover usually triggers after 24 hours
of sitting with no dispatched miles.
Typical rates run $100 to $175 per 24
hour cycle with some carriers paying
anywhere from 50 to $200 a day.
>> Detention is waiting at a dock.
Layover is waiting for the next load.
Confuse the two on a claim and you can
leave thousands of dollars on the table
over the course of a year.
>> Then there's the third category,
accessorial pay.
Accessorials are all the extra charges
beyond the line haul rate. The pay for
everything the load demands besides
driving.
>> Truck ordered not used, when you show up
and the load cancels.
Lumper fees, when you pay someone to
unload the trailer.
Tarping a flatbed.
Extra stops.
Redelivery.
Fuel surcharge.
Each one is money if it is in writing.
>> Take truck ordered not used.
You deadhead 200 miles to a shipper and
the load cancels.
Without a tonu clause, you just drove
200 unpaid miles.
With one, you collect a flat fee that
covers the wasted trip.
>> Or lumper fees.
You pay $100 out of pocket for someone
to unload your trailer and if nobody
reimburses you, that is $100 straight
out of your settlement.
Always confirm who pays the lumper
before you arrive.
>> The pattern is the same every time.
If it is not in the rate confirmation,
it does not exist. Accessorial pay only
becomes real when it is written down
before the work happens.
Here is the scale of the problem
nationally.
In 2018, the Department of
Transportation's Office of Inspector
General studied driver detention, and
the numbers were staggering.
>> Detention costs for hired truckload
drivers between 1.1 and 1.3 billion
dollars a year in lost earnings. That is
billion with a B, every single year.
>> Per driver, the report estimated between
1281 and 1534 dollars a year just
evaporated at docks. And carriers lose
another 250 to 300 million in net
income.
>> It is also a safety crisis.
The same report found that a 15-minute
increase in average dwell time raises
the expected crash rate by 6.2%.
>> Think about why.
A driver paid by the mile loses money
every minute he sits.
So, he makes it up by speeding, pushing
his hours, driving tired.
The unpaid wait at the dock becomes a
safety risk on the highway.
>> And the waits are not short. An
owner-operator Independent Drivers
Association survey found more than 30%
of members spend 11 to 20 hours per week
in detention.
>> 11 to 20 hours.
Every week.
That is up to half a work week unpaid
sitting at facilities. 31% said they
lose three to four loads a month because
detention wrecked their schedule.
>> Some drivers reported detention costing
them more than $6,000 a month.
Read that again.
$6,000 a month lost to waiting.
>> So, why does this keep happening?
Because the first two hours are free,
and free gets consumed.
One industry analyst put it bluntly.
It is unsurprising that retailers would
consume every minute of that free time.
>> There is no incentive to hurry. The
shipper's warehouse is not paying for
your time during those two hours. So,
your time is the cheapest resource in
the building.
Of course, they use all of it.
>> And here's the part that should make
every driver angry.
The facilities that are notorious for
slow loading end up having to pay above
market rates to attract carriers, plus
detention charges of 25 to $100 an hour
or more.
>> So, the money exists. The slow shippers
do pay, eventually, to somebody.
The question is whether any of it
reaches the driver who actually sat
there.
>> Which brings us to the most important
part of this episode.
How drivers actually collect detention
pay.
Because the money is real, the clause is
real, and most of it goes unclaimed.
>> Step one happens before you ever drive
to the shipper.
The detention clause must be in the rate
confirmation before you accept the load.
The rate, the free time, the increments,
all spelled out.
>> If the rate confirmation says nothing
about detention, you've already lost the
negotiation.
One veteran driver puts it simply.
If your rate confirmation does not spell
out detention before you accept the
load, you already lost.
>> Step two is the timestamp. The moment
you arrive, you notify the broker or
your dispatcher in writing with the
time. Not a phone call.
Something with a timestamp.
>> Step three is the warning shot.
You send that notice before your free
time expires, not after.
The notice that says detention is now
accruing puts the broker on the clock
and creates your paper trail.
>> Step four is the bill of lading.
Get your in and out times written on the
BOL and initialed by someone at the
facility. Keep your gate tickets and
receipts. Photograph everything.
>> Step five is the follow-up.
Billed detention that is never invoiced
is never paid.
You submit the claim with your
documentation attached, and you follow
up until it is on your settlement.
>> Here is the hard truth about step five.
Industry guidance is blunt about it. If
your logs and your bills of lading are
not watertight, your claim may go
unpaid. Documentation is the entire
game.
>> Now, a word for company drivers, because
this is where it gets uncomfortable.
When a shipper pays detention to the
carrier, does the driver see any of it?
>> Sometimes yes, sometimes no.
Some carriers pass detention straight
through to the driver.
Others keep it, or pay the driver a
smaller amount than the shipper paid the
carrier.
It depends entirely on the company's
policy.
>> So, ask.
Ask your carrier what the detention
pass-through policy is, in writing.
If they collect $60 an hour from the
shipper and pay you 20, you deserve to
know that before you sit at the dock.
>> Owner-operators have the same homework
with brokers.
Know the detention terms before you book
the load, because after you are sitting
at the dock, your leverage is gone.
>> Let us talk about what fair even means.
Some drivers argue detention should
equal what they would earn driving.
If you make a dollar a mile at 60 miles
an hour, that is $60 an hour of lost
income before expenses.
>> Others say it should be higher, because
sitting still also burns your 14-hour
clock, which can cost you the next load
entirely.
One driver told a trade publication that
detention should be what you make
driving down the road, $100 plus.
>> The Owner-Operator Independent Drivers
Association goes further.
They argue the whole 2-hour free concept
discounts the value of a driver's time,
and that shippers should not get a
complimentary grace period at the
driver's expense.
>> Whatever the right number is, the
direction is clear.
Your time has a price, and every hour
you give away for free is an hour you
will never get back.
>> Let us put a bow on the math.
A driver who loses just 5 hours a week
past free time at $60 an hour is giving
away $300 a week.
>> That is $15,600
a year for sitting still.
In a paid parking lot.
That is the real cost of not knowing how
this system works.
>> So, here's your checklist.
Get the detention clause in the rate
confirmation before you accept.
Timestamp your arrival in writing.
Send notice before free time ends.
>> Get in and out times on the bill of
lading initialed by the facility. Keep
every receipt.
Invoice it and follow up until it lands
on your settlement.
>> And know your carrier's pass-through
policy.
The money is in the system.
The only question is whether it ends up
in your pocket or someone else's.
>> Detention, layover, and accessorial pay
are not bonuses.
They are wages for hours you already
worked.
Collect them like it.
>> Next time on Trucking Business
Explained, we go back to where it all
started.
The 1980 law that blew up the entire
industry.
The rise and fall of American Trucking.
See you there.

metadata.shortDescription:
In this video, we'll discuss the broker's responsibility for detention and how brokers not paying affects drivers. We discuss customers who do not pay detention. We'll also discuss how much drivers are typically paid for detention and my opinion on how much they should be paid. 
I give tips to drivers and dispatchers on what to ask to make sure you get paid detention. 

Drivers who experience long delays or cancellations are usually entitled to compensation from their broker. This compensation is called detention.
Carriers, demand your money and get it in writing!

For free training on how to become a (ethical) freight broker, go to icantremember.com 
Subscribe for more free logistics videos.

metadata.author: Freight 360

Detention is common in trucking, but what is it?  Why do we pay for it?  And how can we limit how often it’s paid?  In this video, I'm going to break it all down for you.

metadata.title: How Freight Brokers Handle Detention And Rate Issues!
metadata.author: Brandon Scott
metadata.shortDescription:
In this video today Brandon is discussing 2 BIG issues freight brokers & truckers disagree & whose to blame!

😀 You'll  learn 
What is detention pay (scenario)
Who pays detention (freight broker/shipper)
Why freight brokers and truckers have issues with rates and detention (accessorial charges)
Whose to blame for detention and rate issues 
How to solve these issues 

Check this video out and learn how to develop WINNING relationships with carriers!

Comments Welcome!

Want to learn more about the freight broker business?

😀 Check out my FREE 5 Video Series: "How The Load Movement Process Works"  

1. Click Here... https://brandonthefreightbroker.com
​​​​2. Wait for the scroll-down to appear 
3. Enter your name and email 
4. Click submit
5. Check your email (spam/junk) for first video

See you at the top because the bottom is much too crowded!

why freight brokers and truckers disagree
2 big issues freight broker and truckers disagree

Because remember when a trucker's wheels are not rolling he's not making any money. So this money compensates him for his time, so to speak, okay? So now the detention policy that is in place or should be in place is the broker's detention policy because the broker has a relationship with the carrier. It is not the carrier that has a relationship with the shipper. The shipper has a relationship with the broker. So the broker and the carrier will have what we call a detention policy. So it outlines what happens when detention takes place. Now, if you don't have a detention policy in place is a very real possibility that you don't get paid detention if you're a carrier, if the broker doesn't have that policy in place. So it is your responsibility as the carrier we're getting ready to assign some responsibility here. It is your responsibility as a carrier to make sure that your broker has a detention policy in place. And he pays detention after a certain thing happens. For example, say you were at a facility, you have been there three hours every hour after the third hour, you may get detention pay. If there's no policy in place that says that there's a chance that you won't get it. My responsibility is to have a detention policy. Again, we're assigning some responsibility. We gave some responsibility to the carrier. His responsibility is to make sure that there's a policy in place. The broker's responsibility is a negotiator. He has to negotiate with the shipper if the shipper does not have a policy already for detention to have a policy in place. Because this is important to the broker, this is important to his relationship with the carrier. He has to make sure that he takes care of his carrier by having a detention policy in place, because he knows that sometimes hours are gonna be extended at those facilities. And when they are, at least he can compensate his carrier because remember the carrier is your partner. This is your team member, you're working together. So you don't want your team member out in the cold not getting paid when he should get paid. So as the broker, I'm gonna make sure there's a policy in place with the shipper and I that says, this is what happens when detention takes place. Yes, the shipper is going to pay it. He will pay that amount, whatever it is, but it's my job as a freight broker to make sure that that policy is in place. So, when I'm talking to the carrier about detention I already know he and I already know what the detention policy is, what the detention rate is. Now it's just about saying, "Hey, let's get a new rate confirmation and give you the detention hours that you've accumulated." Carriers have to get paid detention. If they don't, then that doesn't look very good for the broker. It also doesn't look very good for the carrier because you aren't negotiating a very important piece of the contract. All carriers should make sure that there's a detention policy in place if you wanna get paid detention. What is the detention policy? Is a question that we should be asking as a carrier. And as a broker the question that I should be asking my shipper, what is your detention policy? So I can draw up a contract that reflects my policy based off of what my shippers policy is to ensure my carrier gets paid. That is making sure we're taking care of carriers. And the carrier has to make sure he take care of himself by enforcing those policies, making sure that those policies exist. Number one, and then when it's time to get paid, get paid on that policy, get those rate confirmation changed out to make sure you get paid because the contract says already that you're getting paid. So there's nothing to worry about with that part that's done already. But, if it's not done, then you have a problem. So that's what I'm talking about when I'm saying there is responsibility on both sides for the broker to do his job to make sure there's a policy already in place that exists between he and the shipper. And then the carrier do to do his job to say, "Hey broker, where is the detention policy?" I need to know what happens when detention takes place. And one thing to remember is that when a broker is requesting approval from a shipper he's really requesting that approval for himself. Because in order for the broker to pay a detention he wants to be able to get paid from the shipper to pay you that detention which is the right thing to do because you do have to get an approval for detention simply basically by explaining the situation. This is what took place. Carrier arrived on time and it's past the time limit and he still hasn't gotten unloaded just yet. So, we would just, you know, sending this email to make sure that we could get approved for detention, give them the PO number. Then they'll send you back. PO number has been approved for detention and you turn that in, when you get ready to turn your invoice in to make sure you get paid. But, if you have that policy in place your carrier is already getting paid. You pay that with the invoice. When you get that receipt from the shipper saying that the detention has been approved. Now the overall invoice is going to be paid to include detention rate. That's how it works. Okay, so the next issue that we're gonna discuss is probably one of the biggest issues between freight brokers and carriers, and that is rates. What is a rate? A rate is simply saying, what a broker is paying a shipper to move a load from point A to point B. Then I take that number and I say, okay, I have $1000 in the load. So I wanna go to the carrier at $800 in order for me to make $200 on the load. So the rate is $1,000. The rate that I'm paying to the carrier is $800. And the difference my profit is $200 on that load. So that's what a rate is. Now, why is there so many problems around rates? Well, carriers are always going to think a lot of times that the freight broker has more in the lane than he's offering. And a lot of times he may have more in a lane sometimes he may not have more. But for my experience, most times, you know, carriers think that freight brokers have way more in the lane than they actually have. And that's, you know, causes some problems there because the carrier is saying, "Hey I think you have a little bit more, so I want a little bit more from the pot." Which is understandable. But in most cases, at least in my experience, those rates are not nearly as high as you're thinking in most cases. Now, yes, there are gonna be times when rates go up and we have some leverage and we can make some things happen in those lanes and get better rates. But for my experience, again, usually those rates are probably two to $500 caution in those rates. And a lot of times closer to the 200 mark depending on how good the freight broker is at bidden lanes, at pricing, at negotiating, because that's what this thing is all about. When it boils down to it the freight broker is going to the shipper and he's often a rate based off of his experience. Now, if you have a rookie freight broker, then sometimes you're gonna have some very, very low rates in those lanes because they may not be using leverage. They may not have that leverage just yet. They may not have that experience of bidden lanes and they bid too low trying to get the lane and then they bring a weak rate to the market. And now you have a carrier that probably is not gonna take that rate. So that's what rates are. That's why we have so many problems around rates because there always seems to be a little bit more to the carrier in the rate. And then that negotiation goes on. But once we negotiate and we come up with a price that you and I can agree on the broker and the carrier we've said, "Hey, this rate will work." And I send you out a rate confirmation and that rate confirmation is signed. You move the load, that one is done, it's finished. What usually happens is other people say, that a carrier shouldn't move a load based on this rate or that rate, but you are not that carrier. You're not in that situation. So it probably, you know, you probably wouldn't be the best person to try and give advice to what the carrier should do because the carrier knows what he should do. It's his own situation. So, you know, when it comes down to bidding on lanes and rates that's something that, you know, you're gonna get better at as time goes. But also the carrier has a responsibility here too to get the rate that is good for him and his truck because if he is not profitable then he can't stay in business either. So the carrier has some responsibility and the broker has responsibility when it comes to rates. We cannot assign the responsibility to one person. And I think that what happens a lot of times people say, "Oh the broker is the problem with rates." Or somebody say, "The carrier is a problem." No, they both are the problem. The broker has to understand that the carrier is a team member. The carrier has to understand that also and treat each other like team members. So when I go out and start to negotiate on a rate I'm negotiating for the best rate, because I know that I have to get a piece of that pie. And my carrier has to get the lion's share. And it has to be sufficient. It has to be enough money so that he can keep his truck moving. And of course have some money to put in pocket because this is a profit game. This is not just about making money. That is what confuses a lot of people, a lot of time, you get the idea, you're making money because money is coming in. What are you truly making when you move a load from point A to point B? How much gas are you spending? What is your time worth? So when you're coming up with rates you have to get a rate that is good for you. That is good for your business. And when you do that and you agree to that then we send you out a rate con, we sign that rate con and we move the load, and that's it. But at the end of the day, nobody is twisting each other arm to take a rate, that is totally and completely up to that carrier whether he's gonna take a rate or he's not gonna take a rate. And also the broker, it's gonna be up to him to make sure that he's coming to his carrier with a solid rate. Because people aren't working for pennies. And why this is so important is because I don't own trucks. So if I don't treat the people that own trucks in a way that's respectful that they can say, you know what? I can see the value in Brandon and Alliance Logistics. If truckers can not see that then they won't be working with me for long. Okay, so the last thing that I wanna leave you with is that there's plenty of blame to go around. We can always look to blame someone else for problems that we're having in our own business. At the end of the day, if your business is not doing well it's the business owner's fault. What we understand is that as entrepreneurs, it's not about looking for someone else to blame something on because it's my fault. If my business is not going the way that I want it to go, if it's not making the profits that I wanted to make, if it's not making the impact that I wanted to make then it's my own fault. And I have to do something about it in order to change the outcome. If I don't do anything about it, if I look for someone else to blame, then it's very likely the problem is never going to get fixed because I'm not addressing the root cause of the problem. And the root cause is me. If my business is going wrong so I have to fix those problems. That's the same with the truck driver. That's the same with any other freight broker. If a problem exists, then it's the business owner's fault. He must get down to the bottom of it in order to fix it. So that's what I wanted to share with you today. You'll get to see me in my office moving freight talking to carriers, talking to shippers. So check the description for the link. Thank you so much for spending some of your time with me today. I wish you the very best in your life in business. See you at the top because the bottom is much too crowded.

metadata.shortDescription:
On today’s episode, Kevin and guest co-host Richie Daigle, from our SONAR sales team, discuss the inner workings of freight brokerages. We go from the popular business models to what is worrying freight brokerages the most in 2021.  We welcome Justin Wandell, General Manager of Axle Logistics, to the show. We’ll break down the sales strategy for cradle to grave and how it differs from the buy/sell model. Plus, listener feedback, advice, and community building!

metadata.title: How Cold Calls and Customer Service Built a $50M Freight Brokerage
metadata.author: FreightCaviar
metadata.shortDescription:
Freight brokerage founder John Ferguson breaks down how Pivot Supply Chain Solutions grew to $50M, why cold calling and customer service still win in logistics, and where AI fits into the future of freight brokerage.

John also opens up about how freight brokering changed his life, from spending time in foster care and struggling as a young adult to building a career, a family, and his own company. Now, after checking off many of the milestones he set for himself, he says the next thing left to chase is a $1B freight brokerage.

This week's episode is sponsored by Epay Manager, Goodship, Highway, and Bitfreighter.

Interested in sponsoring our podcast? Send us an email at pbj@freightcaviar.com

Launch your freight brokerage with my mentorship: https://freightframeworks.com/go/5dd8c9a2
Free 58-minute freight broker training: https://freightframeworks.com/go/6eae7799

The exact sales system to take a freight brokerage from $0 to $10K a month: ditch the volume fallacy, specialize so you're not a commodity, and lock in 3 golden lanes at $300 profit per load. You'll also learn the land and expand strategy and how to build a carrier fortress that protects your margins.

1:47 – The Power of Specialization
3:09 – The Golden Lane Strategy
4:54 – Land & Expand: Turning One Lane Into Six Figures
6:04 – Building Your Carrier Fortress
7:36 – Final Step: Securing Your First Client

Launch your freight brokerage with my mentorship: https://freightframeworks.com/go/a1effa22
Free 58-minute freight broker training: https://freightframeworks.com/go/70aaf071

The untold reality of becoming a freight broker: it's not a suit-and-high-rise job, it's a grind of networking, negotiating, and solving problems from your kitchen table. The legal side, FMCSA authority and a surety bond, is teachable but slow, and when trucks break down or weather hits, you're the firefighter. Freedom is great, but there's no steady paycheck, so ask yourself if you can handle the uncertainty.

On this episode of WHAT THE TRUCK?!?, host Thomas Watson teams up with special guest Malcolm Harris of Axle Logistics to dig into the wild world of freight brokerage. From declining freight volumes and tightening driver availability to game-changing mergers in the rail industry, they break down the state of the supply chain with insight and humor.

Also joining the show is Will Jenkins, CEO and founder of Journey, who shares his playbook for building high-performing brokerage teams, why training is essential to retention, and how success is defined across recruiting, consulting, and carrier partnerships.

Expect honest takes on tough markets, real stories from the trenches, and laughs along the way. Whether you're a broker, a driver, or just freight-curious, this episode is a full load.

And so over time they became more polished and they became better presenters and they got better at certain aspects of it, but they simply didn't stop selling. And so you think about the amount of effort it takes to move an opportunity from prospect to close one and then to expand that. There are multiple emails, multiple phone calls. We did a study across our clients on the consulting side and it takes typically an average of seven to 10 touches via email and you can sprinkle in obviously your phone calls and things of that nature, face to face meetings um before that customer reciprocates, right? And so if you get hung up on or you send an email and it bounces back or that person doesn't respond, we're just starting the game, right? This is a marathon. So I need to stay on it and be as persistent as possible. The second level of that is am I talking to the right types of people and are those the types of customers that my business transacts with successfully? And so if you're talking to the right people long enough, man, there's going to be some people that don't believe me, but like sales is is a numbers game, right? I do want to have the right types of customers. My messaging needs to be correct. But early on in my career, I need to be in front of the right types of people persistently until an opportunity comes up. Um, and a lot of times we see people kind of give up before they get to that finish line or really close and they stop because, you know, they get told no. And as a seller yourself, you have to be okay with ambiguity early on. And then as an organization, you have to go and find a handful of people that have done it before and are willing to work through that ambiguity knowing where you're going to get. But it is not easy, right? Like I remember, you know, zero to 20 and 20 to 100. There were just people that we wanted to hire or customers that we were going after that just wouldn't give us the time of day. Um, and obviously that's a challenge, but you need to be able to persist through that. As you as you grow, you get more recognition, your brand becomes more well-known. Gets a little bit easier. It's not easy. It just is easier. Early on though, you have to be okay as a seller knowing that all the pieces aren't put together and you can somewhat shoot from the hip, but like that's part of being a startup. And then you start to build some recognition um and it becomes a little bit easier. >> Definitely. I know uh I want to be mindful of of your time with us, but I I had one more question for you. Um you know, looking ahead, you are obviously in the heart of Chicago, but you are the heart of Journey. what is ahead for you and the rest of that fabulous team that you have in the trenches with you every day? >> Yes. So, we will be releasing a new tier of the training that we do. I won't tease too much of it, but it'll be geared more towards owners and founders. Uh we do a ton of consulting and that's onetoone but often times we find that in group settings there's a lot of value to be derived based on having good conversations about where your business is and where it can go. Uh so that's going to be an element of what we'll be uh marketing here shortly because we think there's broad application to some of the business fundamentals that we teach a lot of our consulting clients and we want to be able to make a broader impact. So um you'll see a little bit of that from us which I think becomes a pretty big staple of one of our our service offerings. >> That's awesome. Will that's awesome. And um do you have any other questions? >> Oh no. I just wanted to thank you so much for coming on and thank you so much for your time as well. Uh we'll definitely once you guys get that released, let us know. We'll have you back on and we'll definitely catch up again soon. >> Appreciate it. Thank you very much for your time. >> Thank you so much, Will. >> Man, he is uh he's awesome, man. He's got the best squad, but he's also got the best quads. Like I'm very jealous. Like >> And he's got the best quads, too. Oh, yeah. >> Yeah. Like the dude is a tank, man. I'm like, brother. like go help Michael Pennix win the Falcons a championship. Like let this go. Let this lifestyle go. We don't we we're good. You've you've done more than you have ever been asked. No, he's he's amazing. One thing I think that there's a lot of trucking lore and stuff, but the brokerage space has lore as well. And that's one of the the one of the coolest things. It's like Beethoven met this person who met this person who met this person who met Donald Trump who met Kanye West who met Lil Uzi Ver. >> No way. So it's like 10 degrees of Kevin Bacon. >> Yes. Yes. That is what logistics in our industry is like. So for me I got my start literally 6 months as soon as I graduated from college at the University of Tennessee. Go VSS of course. >> Um >> man I was renting cars and I saw my best friend that I worked with at the time. They got me at the career fair and I was like, man, I can't allow this to happen to somebody else. So, I ended up getting into logistics. Like, yeah, like getting him to like and his family, you know, I've driven around a lot of different players, players that we've lost. We just didn't have the system. But that's really how I got my start is is it was a chance. The energy and the buzz at that time at Coyote Logistics was is something that was unreal. I mean it truly felt like a PG version of Wolf Wall Street if you get my so it was fun. I mean, there's a guy uh he's still in Chattanooga, and I'll shout him out. His name's Klay Hicks. Taught me how to be a pro. It's like, for example, um and I'm a Falcons guy. Julio Jones his rookie year was like, "Listen, I would have been out of the league if it wasn't for Rody White. I tried to put the the chicken wings down and I I've tried to, you know, just mirror that. And then also, I mean, currently, I mean, there's a a leader I have, Ally Freillley. the way she is operationally efficient and thinking about all right hey I'm three moves ahead and seeing that on a people side I mean it's like literally operation in terms of freight and logistics but she's thinking of it in terms of training and development and being able to properly like cultivate a culture that is going to just carry on it's like at Axel we think 90 days out >> that is just a staple and just to have that vision and that that foresight to be like all right like this is where we're at, dude. It's always going to be like this. It's cynical, right? Like it always is going to go up and down. And you have to then rely on what your skill set staying even kill and knowing, all right, I have to be creative with my approach. I have to be diligent in my attack. Such as Will's point. Like he is saying like, hey, like you have to have a certain skill set, but also like know who you're talking to. Like it's just like don't don't phone it in just for the metrics, right? Like the barber. >> Yes, the barber analogy. So, you got to pay for your seat because say for example, a barber um you know, it's $1,000 for rent and then everything after that is for them to to spend. It's like that in a brokerage. And you know typical models like you know at Access it's uh you know the the 40k model and I've seen that in quite a few is like all right 40k is like the benchmark of a good salesperson of a quality healthy book of business and having that model so that you can have other pods and grow and build and expand like that is the goal and if you're not at least trending that way I mean either a you have to have a conversation about hey what am I doing wrong or b you have to have a conversation like yo is this for me like is this genuinely for me? >> Final thoughts. metadata.title: Do you have what it takes to build a freight brokerage?
metadata.author: Matt Krause
metadata.shortDescription:
Launch your freight brokerage with my mentorship: https://freightframeworks.com/go/72671d69
Free 58-minute freight broker training: https://freightframeworks.com/go/73414cbc

Do you have what it takes to build a freight brokerage? The unfiltered look at the job: it's operationally heavy, stuff goes wrong daily, and you'll need thick skin for 30 to 50 dials a day. If you can stay calm when a truck catches fire and keep dialing after 49 no's, the $800B truckload market has room for you.

0:00 – Who Matt is and what it means to be an independent freight broker.
0:43 – Typical day as a freight broker and operational challenges.
1:15 – Handling chaotic situations like truck breakdowns.
1:46 – Importance of resilience and dealing with rejection.
2:30 – Matt’s personal story of landing his first deal after multiple rejections.
3:38 – Staying calm in high-pressure situations.
4:12 – Managing customer communication during crises.
5:18 – Why organization is essential.
5:50 – Financial expectations for a freight broker in the first year.
6:27 – Scaling your brokerage versus working a 9-to-5 job.
7:27 – The massive opportunity in the $800 billion truckload market.
8:29 – Matt’s offer to help build a $300,000 freight brokerage or agency within a year.

One of the biggest questions in freight brokerage is simple:

How do you actually get customers?

In this video, I break down how freight brokers really find and land shippers, what works in today’s market, and what most people get wrong when trying to build a book of business.

You’ll learn:
• How to identify the right types of shippers to target  
• Where to actually find freight customers  
• The role cold outreach plays in building your book  
• Why most brokers fail at follow-up  
• How to position yourself without competing on price  
• What it takes to build a consistent pipeline of freight  

This isn’t about theory — it’s about how customer acquisition actually works in freight brokerage.

Some people try to learn this through trial and error.

Others want speed, certainty, and structure from day one.

If you want to learn more about building a freight brokerage the right way, visit:

👉 freightbrokerbusinessacademy.com

👍 Like and subscribe for more real-world freight and logistics insights.

A lot of beginners wonder if it is too late to become a freight broker or freight agent. They see more competition, bigger brokers, load boards, AI tools, and shippers who already have transportation providers, and they start to think they may have missed their shot.

FREE DOWNLOAD: Grab my free cheat sheet, How to Become A Freight Broker in 7 Simple Steps.

In this video, I break down why freight brokerage is still a real opportunity for beginners who are willing to learn the business, choose a niche, build a prospect list, improve their sales skills, and solve real problems for shippers.

* What I would focus on if I were starting today

metadata.title: The Economics of Owning a Freight Brokerage
metadata.author: The Finance Pro
metadata.shortDescription:
The Economics of Owning a Freight Brokerage

How Freight Brokers Actually Make Money
The Hidden Math of a Freight Brokerage: Thin Spreads, Late Checks, Big Risks
Owning a Freight Brokerage: The Dream vs. the Real Economics
Freight Brokerage Explained: The Business Model Behind America’s Trucking Middlemen
Why a Profitable Freight Broker Can Still Go Broke

Okay, so you want to own a freight brokerage. Find a truck, take a cut of every load, and watch the money roll in. That’s the dream version, and it’s not entirely wrong. But the real economics are a lot stranger.

In this documentary, we follow one aspiring broker through the real mechanics of the business: the thin spread between what shippers pay and what carriers earn, the cash gap that can sink a profitable company, and the legal and fraud risks that keep getting bigger.

🔎 In this video you’ll learn:

How a freight broker makes money on the spread
Why shippers and carriers get paid on very different timelines
What the $75,000 federal bond actually is (and isn’t)
How quick pay and factoring work
Why growth can drain a brokerage’s cash
How fraud, double brokering, and cargo theft hit the middleman
What the 2026 Supreme Court ruling in Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II means for brokers
What the numbers from C.H. Robinson’s Q3 2026 results show about scale
Why C.H. Robinson’s planned acquisition of RXO matters

📚 SOURCES & NOTES
This video draws on company earnings releases (C.H. Robinson Q3 2026), FMCSA registration requirements, court coverage of Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II (May 14, 2026), Verisk CargoNet cargo theft reports, and industry trade press. Industry market-size estimates vary widely by definition and are treated as rough. Small-brokerage figures (margins, cash gap, quick-pay fees) are examples from industry guides and modeling, not audited data. Some arithmetic is the creator’s own, based on reported figures.

⚠️ DISCLAIMER
This video is for educational purposes only and is not financial, legal, or investment advice. Always check current sources and consult a qualified professional before making business or financial decisions.

#FreightBrokerage #BusinessEconomics #Trucking

HOW TO GET YOUR (BMC-84) SURETY BOND – STEP-BY-STEP GUIDE! 🚛💰

If you’re starting a freight brokerage business, securing a BMC-84 surety bond is a crucial step! 🏆 This bond, required by the FMCSA (Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration), ensures that you comply with regulations and protect motor carriers and shippers from financial loss. In this video, we’ll walk you through the process of obtaining your BMC-84 surety bond quickly and efficiently! 📜✅

What is a BMC-84 Surety Bond? 🤔

A BMC-84 bond is a $75,000 surety bond required by the FMCSA for freight brokers and freight forwarders to legally operate. It acts as a financial guarantee that brokers will fulfill their contractual obligations. If a broker fails to pay carriers or shippers, a claim can be made against the bond. This protects motor carriers and shippers while keeping the industry fair and trustworthy. 🚛🔒

How to Get Your BMC-84 Surety Bond 📝

The process of obtaining a BMC-84 bond is simple but requires a few key steps:
1️⃣ Find a reputable surety bond provider – Choose a company that specializes in FMCSA bonds for the best rates and service. 💼
2️⃣ Submit an application – Provide details about your brokerage, including your financial history and credit score. 📑
3️⃣ Get a bond quote – Your credit score and financial health will determine the cost, typically ranging from $900 to $2,500 per year. 💵
4️⃣ Sign the agreement and pay the premium – Once approved, you’ll receive your bond, which will then be filed with the FMCSA. ✅

BMC-84 Surety Bond vs. BMC-85 Trust Fund 📊

Many brokers wonder whether to get a BMC-84 surety bond or opt for a BMC-85 trust fund. While a BMC-85 requires putting up the full $75,000 in a trust account, a BMC-84 bond only requires an annual premium. This makes the surety bond a more affordable option for new brokers looking to minimize upfront costs. 💰🔄

Final Tips for Freight Brokers 🚚

Getting your BMC-84 surety bond is just one step in launching a successful freight brokerage. Ensure you also complete your FMCSA registration, get your freight broker authority, and build strong relationships with shippers and carriers. 📦🔗 Watch this video to learn how to secure your BMC-84 bond with ease and start your journey as a freight broker today! 🚀

🔔 Don't forget to LIKE, COMMENT, and SUBSCRIBE for more freight industry tips and business strategies! 🚛📈 #FreightBroker #BMC84Bond #SuretyBond #FreightBrokerAuthority #TruckingBusiness #Logistics

segments.text: An Essential Guide to Freight Broker Bonds
Before discussing what a Freight Broker Bond is, let’s first understand what a Freight Broker is.
A freight broker, sometimes referred to as a third-party logistic firm, is a regulated
company licensed to contract with motor carriers to move freight for their shipping customers.
They basically do the negotiating and transacting and delivers the freight where it needs to be.
Some of the duties of freight brokers include, but are not limited to:
• Finding shippers and carriers • Keeping records of each transaction
(like contracts, payables, receivables, etc.) • Setting appropriate rates for each freight load
• Moving freight
What is a Freight Broker Bond?
A Freight Broker Bond is a requirement of the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration
(FCMSA) and must be obtained before a license is issued to the freight broker.
It ensures that freight brokers and forwarders maintain certain
standards and follow the regulations of the FMCSA. It also serves to prevent fraudulent
activities and guarantees timely payments and compensation to motor carriers and shippers.
A surety bond always has 3 parties. In this case, the freight broker is known as the Principal,
the FMCSA is the Obligee, and the Surety company is the underwriter of the bond.
If the freight brokers fail to meet their obligations,
then the FCMSA can file a claim against the bond. The surety company will investigate the claim,
and if it is found to be valid, then payment will be made to the FMCSA.
The freight broker will then be responsible for paying back the
surety company for the amount that was paid out of the claim.
How much does a Freight Broker Bond cost?
The bond cost, referred to as the bond premium,
is only a percentage of the bond amount, which can typically range between 1%-10%.
The cost is based on the applicant's credit standing and financial and professional capacity.
How do you obtain a Freight Broker Bond?
To secure a Freight Broker Bond, just simply follow these steps:
1. Find a trusted and experienced surety bond provider that offers this type of surety bond.
2. The surety underwriter may need some information
about your personal financial situation. 3. The application is simple and a surety
agent will contact you to go over any necessary documents to complete the bond paperwork.
4. You will pay your premium and your bond documents will be sent to you right away.
Ultimately, the goal of freight broker bonds is to guarantee that brokering is
an ethical and fair industry where the people involved earn rightful payments for their work.
At the same time, surety bonds offer a positive indication for freight brokers
that demonstrate they are financially capable and safe to conduct business with.
If you are in need of a Freight Broker Bond, our surety bond experts can
assist you and provide consulting services for your bonding needs.
Call us at 800-333-7800, or visit our website and get your FREE Quote today!

metadata.title: File a BMC-84 / BMC-85 | Motus Explainer Series
metadata.author: FMCSA
metadata.shortDescription:
Welcome to the Motus Explainer Series! In this video, we provide a clear, step-by-step walkthrough on how to file a BMC-84 (Broker Surety Bond) or BMC-85 (Broker Trust Fund Agreement) using Motus, the modernized USDOT Registration System.
Ensuring your financial responsibility filings are submitted correctly is essential for maintaining your active operating authority. Follow along to learn how to navigate the new interface and submit your documentation seamlessly.

⚠️ Prerequisite: Before you can submit any financial responsibility filings, your organization must be fully registered and logged into an active Supporting Company account in Motus.

In this video, we cover:

0:00 - Introduction & Prerequisites: A quick overview of the bond and trust fund filing process and verifying your supporting company account access.

0:18 - Step 1: Account Foundation: Double-checking your registration baseline before initiating a new transaction.

0:29 - Step 2: Creating a New Filing: How to find the "Manage Filings" dropdown menu at the top of your screen and select "Create New Filing."

0:40 - Step 3: Searching for an Entity: Pinpointing the specific regulated entity using their USDOT Number or Legal Business Name.

0:57 - Step 4: Reviewing Business Information: A crucial compliance checkpoint to verify the company’s name, address, and current filings to prevent making redundant or duplicate submissions.

1:12 - Step 4 (Cont.) & Step 5: Selecting Operating Authority: Selecting the dropdown to choose your authority and observing how the platform dynamically generates the exact form required based on your capabilities.

1:28 - Crucial Pro-Tip (The Single-Filing Rule): A major compliance reminder that a completely separate filing must be submitted for every single individual authority tied to that USDOT number—no bundling allowed!

1:36 - Step 6: Confirming and Submitting: Inputting your policy number, checking the effective date (which automatically defaults to the current date), and completing the submission process.

Keep your financial records aligned and your transportation business safely moving forward!

Helpful Links:
Access the Motus System: https://motus.dot.gov/
Ask FMCSA: https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/registration/ask-fmcsa 
Learn more about the USDOT Registration System modernization: https://www.fmcsa.dot.gov/registration/resources-hub

 #Motus #USDOT #BMC84 #BMC85 #BrokerBond #FreightBroker #TruckingCompliance #TransportationModernization

segments.text: What commission percentage do freight
brokers get paid? There's a bunch of
variables that go into answering this
question, so let's take a look at a few
of the common freight brokering jobs and
how much commission they earn.
Hey everyone, I'm Nate Cross with
Freight 360. And in today's video, we're
talking all about that sweet sweet thing
called commission.
We know how freight brokers make money,
but how much of that money do they
actually get to keep as a commission?
If you're new here, please hit that
subscribe button down below and make
sure to add the Freight 360 podcast to
your library wherever you listen to
great podcasts.
When it comes to the amount of profit a
freight broker earns, and even more so
the percentage of that money that they
actually keep, it mostly depends on the
business model they're working in. The
three main business models for brokering
freight are as follows. Owning a freight
brokerage, being an agent for a freight
brokerage, and being an employee of a
freight brokerage. In all three of these
business models, the same work is being
performed, but not necessarily by the
same one person. Let's take a look at
each one of these and what percentage
they get to keep.
First up is the brokerage owner. A
freight broker that owns their own
brokerage is licensed directly with the
FMCSA.
Since they own their own company, they
don't receive a commission percentage,
but rather they keep 100% of the
company's profit. Although this might
sound enticing, they are responsible for
many costs associated with running their
business such as insurance, software,
and factoring just to name a few. They
also have to perform the administrative
duties associated with running a
brokerage in addition to just brokering
freight. When scaled in size, licensed
brokerage owners can earn a very good
income.
Next is freight agents.
A freight agent is not a licensed
broker, but instead, they are an
independent contractor that represents
the licensed broker. The licensed
broker, usually a mid-size company,
maintains the legal authority, bond, and
insurance, while the day-to-day
brokering is conducted by the freight
agent or group of freight agents.
The agent works from their home office
and merely focuses on getting freight
from their shippers and matching those
shipments with carriers to move them.
All other back office tasks are
completed by the licensed brokerage
company.
These tasks generally include billing,
collections, claims, cash flow,
marketing, IT support, agent
development, and sometimes pricing and
dispatching services. Since agents don't
perform all of the tasks that go into
running a brokerage, they don't keep all
of the profits.
Agents are generally on a commission
split that will vary around 50 to 70%.
This means for every $1 of profit that
they produce, they earn around 50 to 70
cents.
The licensed brokerage company keeps the
other 30 to 50% to run its back office
operations and for profit.
With such a high commission percentage
offered to freight agents, a brokerage
will usually require the agents to be
experienced and already have an
established customer base before they
are offered an opportunity to join the
brokerage as a new freight agent.
Finally, employees.
Also referred to as W-2 brokers, this is
the most common freight broker in the
market.
There are a lot of large freight broker
companies that operate using this model.
Some examples of large companies that
use this model are TQL, Coyote, and C.H.
Robinson. They might resemble that
boiler room type of sales environment
with thousands of employees. They can
also be much smaller with perhaps only
10 employees or less. In general, the
company has a broker authority from the
FMCSA and hires employees to drive sales
and manage operations. The company owns
the customer accounts, performs all back
office business functions, and furnishes
each employee with an office to work in.
W-2 brokers typically earn a base salary
with a commission directly tied to their
profits. According to a recent
FreightWaves survey, median base pay for
this model is $40,000 base plus an
average commission rate of 13.2%
of gross profits. W-2 brokers make the
lowest commission percentage out of the
three models we've outlined here, but
they are given a base salary, an office
to work in, and job training. You don't
have to have any experience to start as
an employee of a brokerage.
So, there you have it. We've outlined
three different scenarios for brokering
freight and the commission percentage
for these brokers. Which one would you
prefer? Let us know in the comments down
below and we'll see you in the next
video.

metadata.title: How to Be a Freight Agent in 2026 (No Truck, No MC, No Guessing)
metadata.author: Victor Mason
metadata.shortDescription:
Becoming a freight agent is one of the fastest ways to enter the logistics industry without owning trucks, buying equipment, or starting a freight brokerage from scratch.

In this video, I break down exactly what it means to be a freight agent, what the job actually looks like day to day, how freight agents get paid, and how this role is often used as a stepping stone into freight brokerage ownership.

You’ll learn:
• What a freight agent actually is
• The difference between a freight agent and a freight broker
• What freight agents do on a daily basis
• How commission-based pay works in logistics
• Why controlling customers matters more than owning trucks
• How freight agents transition into brokerage ownership

This video is for:
• People looking to enter logistics without high startup costs
• Truck drivers and dispatchers looking to move off the road
• Sales professionals exploring freight and transportation
• Anyone considering freight brokerage but wanting a lower-risk entry point

Some people choose to stay freight agents long term.
Others use the role to learn the business before launching their own brokerage.

If you want to learn more about building a freight business the right way, visit:

https://freightbrokerbusinessacademy.com/webinar-live


📌 Comment “FREIGHT” if you want resources or a roadmap.
👍 Like and subscribe for more real-world freight and logistics content.

@IamVictorMason

metadata.title: Import Containers Explained: From Port Pickup to Empty Return #drayage #portlife #owneroperators
metadata.author: Drayage Academy
metadata.shortDescription:
Import drayage does not end when the freight is delivered.

In this training, I break down the complete import container workflow—from reviewing the Delivery Order and verifying container availability to port pickup, customer delivery, and returning the empty container to the correct location.

You’ll learn why vessel arrival does not mean the container is ready, how Last Free Day affects the shipment, why demurrage must be cleared before the terminal will release the container, and why the steamship line—not the broker—determines where the empty container must be returned.

We’ll also cover:

Delivery Orders
Container availability
Customs and freight releases
Last Free Day
Demurrage
Port pickup requirements
Gate PINs and appointments
Chassis responsibility
Out-gate and in-gate EIRs
Customer delivery documentation
Bill of Lading / POD
Empty-container return locations
Common import mistakes

One of the biggest lessons in import drayage is simple:

Don’t assume. Verify.

Before that truck rolls, confirm the container is available, all required releases are complete, and the terminal is ready to release the load.

📥 FREE DRAYAGE IMPORT CHEAT SHEET

Keep the full import workflow nearby when reviewing and dispatching your next import shipment.

Download here:
https://drayageacademy.com/import-cheat-sheet-request

✅ CHECK YOUR DRAYAGE READINESS SCORE

https://drayageacademy.com/p2p-readiness

🚛 DRAYAGE ACADEMY

Drayage Academy provides practical, real-world training for owner-operators, dispatchers, fleet owners, and trucking companies that want to understand how drayage actually works.

The training is based on more than seven years of hands-on experience operating a drayage trucking company and freight brokerage.

Subscribe for step-by-step training designed to help you operate more confidently and profitably in drayage.

#ImportDrayage #ContainerTrucking #Intermodal #PortTrucking #TruckingEducation

And then step three, confirm the container status on the website is actually available. One quick check can save your driver hours of waiting at the gate just to be turned around without the container. One of the most important dates on an import shipment is the last free date or LFD. The last free date is the final day the container can remain at the terminal or port before daily storage charges begin for your customer. And remember, if your customer hasn't cleared those type charges before you show up, the terminal won't release the container. LFD is important for a carrier when it comes to scheduling the actual pickup date. Storage or demurrage fees are generally not the responsibility of the carrier. Demurrage is paid directly by the party that's responsible for the shipment, not the motor carrier. But the carrier can still be held financially responsible by the customer if the carrier misses the agreed-upon pickup date and then causes the demurrage fees. So don't miss your LFD. That's why checking the terminal's website before dispatching [music] is so important. So for step four, you're not just checking if the container has arrived and if it's available, but also confirm the container's [music] last free date. Once the container is available, now it's time to secure the wheels, >> [music] >> which is step five. Whether you're using your own private chassis or booking one from the chassis pool, confirm your chassis strategy. Do you need a 20-ft chassis or a 40-ft chassis or maybe even a triaxle for overweight containers? If you're getting your chassis from the pool, always save your EIR or equipment [music] interchange receipt. It documents the chassis number, the date and time you received it, [music] and the pickup location. And always inspect the chassis for any visible damages, check the tires, the locking system way before you leave the facility. Because [music] if you leave the facility with damages, it'll be hard to prove later that you didn't cause them. So, now your container is available and you have the wheels. >> [music] >> Now you're ready to head to the port or terminal for your pickup. >> [music] >> Step six is confirming you have your pickup credentials, like the TWIC card, your gate pin, or your rail pickup number. Once your container is loaded on your chassis, >> [music] >> verify the container number and make sure it's sealed, and then make sure those numbers match your delivery order. That's step seven. [music] Upon leaving the terminal, you will receive your outgate >> [music] >> EIR. Just like the chassis EIR, you want to save this with your paperwork. >> [music] >> That's step eight. It documents when and where you took possession of the equipment. Be sure to keep it with your shipment paperwork because most customers will ask for [music] it. Next is delivering the loaded container to the receiver. Step nine. Before arriving to the location, confirm your delivery appointment. Make sure you know your point of contact, the facility hours, any unloading instructions, and the expected wait time to be unloaded. >> [music] >> Make sure you record your arrival and departure times just in case detention becomes necessary, [music] then those times will be extremely important. Once the container has been unloaded, confirm that the receiver has signed the delivery order as proof of your delivery. >> [music] >> The receiver should also provide you with a signed copy as well, which is step 10. Keep your signed copy with your load paperwork along [music] with your EIRs and gate tickets because you'll need them when you invoice your customer. Many carriers think the shipment is finished after the delivery, >> [music] >> but it's not. Now you have to return the empty container, and this is where many drivers get [music] caught off guard. Do not assume the empty container goes back to the same terminal where you picked it up. It's the steamship line that determines where their empty containers are returned. Sometimes the broker knows, sometimes they don't. Sometimes the return location can change while the shipment is in transit. But remember, the carrier remains responsible for the container [music] and the chassis while the equipment is in their possession. So, before the driver leaves the receiver, check with the steamship line to confirm the correct empty return location, which is step 11. If the container is going back to the port, you will need a gate pin in order to engate the empty container. But only return the empty containers to the authorized terminal or facility. And like before, once your empty container is returned, save the ingate EIR [music] with the rest of your load paperwork. That's step 12. One thing I always recommend when you return an empty container to the port [music] is to double-check the port's website to verify the empty has been accepted into their system. >> [music] >> You can look up the status of a container by using your EIR number. Now, if you're returning the chassis back to the chassis pool, keep your chassis in-gate EIR as well. >> [music] >> And trust me, that documentation protects both you and your customer. >> [music] >> I know, I know. There's a lot of steps. If you have questions, please just drop them in the comments below. I will respond. But, here's [snorts] the most important thing to remember. >> [music] >> At every step, save all documents, EIRs, and gate tickets [music] for your records. An import shipment is not complete when you deliver the freight. It is only complete when the empty container has been returned to the authorized location, >> [music] >> accepted by the facility, and supported by your required documentation. Now, to help you stay organized, I created a free drayage import cheat sheet. It includes the complete 12-step process. >> [music] >> It has some important terms you need to know, and a visual road map that follows the shipment from port pickup through empty return. So, [music] use the link in the description to download your free copy. Download it, print it, stick it to your dash. >> [music] >> You can use it whenever you're working an import shipment. Now, if this video helped you better understand the import process, drop [music] a fire emoji in the comments, and make sure you subscribe to the channel. I have a lot more training on the way. >> [music] >> The next video will be on rail freight. We've talked mainly about seaports, but a lot of freight travel on the rail, aka inland ports. So, we'll hit pickup pins, waybills, and grounded containers. [music] So, come back and see me. Thank you so much for watching. Be safe and I'll [music] see you in the next video.

metadata.title: What Is Drayage? Understanding Its Importance in Shipping and Logistics
metadata.author: Drayage Specialist
metadata.shortDescription:
Have you ever wondered how the products you use every day make their way from distant countries to your local stores or warehouses?
In this video, we uncover the vital link in the supply chain known as drayage. Drayage is the short-distance transportation of goods in containers pulled by trucks. It's a key part of the shipping and logistics industry that helps move products from ports and rail terminals to warehouses, distribution centers, or other transportation modes.

In this video, we'll cover:
• What exactly is drayage?
• How drayage fits into the shipping process.
• The importance of drayage in the supply chain.
• Benefits of using a drayage trucking company.

Without efficient drayage services, shipments could get stuck at ports or rail terminals, leading to delays and higher costs. Drayage keeps goods moving smoothly, prevents bottlenecks, and supports just-in-time delivery, helping businesses receive products exactly when they need them.

metadata.author: Freightskills
metadata.shortDescription:
What is container drayage, and how can freight brokers work with it? Learn how import and export containers move between ports, rail yards, and customers, plus the questions to ask before quoting.

Get the free Drayage Checklist: https://freightskills.com/drayage-checklist
Join our free Skool community: https://www.skool.com/freightskills-community-5835

Drayage is more than finding a truck near a port. This lesson follows the container movement, introduces the companies involved, and discusses finding customers and suitable carriers. Use the Drayage Checklist to organize the details you need to investigate before putting a quote together.

IN THIS VIDEO
• Import and export container movements
• Where to look for drayage customers and carriers
• Shipment details and requirements to investigate before quoting

PUT IT TO WORK
Organize container shipment details before quoting. Use the guide alongside this lesson as you work on your own freight business. Join us in the free Freightskills community on Skool to keep learning with other brokers, agents, and logistics professionals.
