metadata.title: Mastering Drayage: A Step by Step Guide for Beginning Freight Brokers
metadata.author: Victor Mason
metadata.shortDescription:
Drayage 101: How Bookings Work, Finding Customers & Tracking Containers (Step-By-Step)

Drayage is one of the most misunderstood but profitable lanes in transportation — and in this video, I break it down from a real-world broker and operator perspective.

If you’ve ever wondered:

How drayage bookings actually work

How brokers and carriers find drayage customers

How to track containers, avoid demurrage, and protect margins

This video is for you.

I walk through the entire drayage lifecycle, from port release to final delivery, so you understand how money is made — and where people usually mess it up.

In this video, you’ll learn:

What drayage really is (and why it’s different from FTL)

How drayage bookings are structured

Where drayage customers come from (importers, exporters, forwarders)

How to win drayage freight without racing to the bottom on price

How to track containers using terminal data, steamship lines, and port systems

Common mistakes that cause demurrage & per diem

How brokers and truckers can both profit in drayage

This is practical, operational knowledge — not theory.

If you’re a:

Freight broker

Truck owner / drayage carrier

Dispatcher

Or someone looking to break into port freight

You need to understand drayage the right way.

👇 Drop a comment if you want a full drayage playbook or training
👍 https://freightbrokerbusinessacademy.com/webinar-live
🔔 Subscribe for more real transportation game

metadata.title: Freight Broker Bond Explained | $75,000 BMC-84 vs BMC-85 | FMCSA Requirements | Bonding Companies
metadata.author: ET Transport
metadata.shortDescription:
🚛 DO YOU REALLY NEED $75,000 TO START A FREIGHT BROKER BUSINESS?

One of the biggest questions new freight brokers ask is whether they need to pay $75,000 upfront to obtain their freight broker authority.

The answer depends on the type of financial security you choose!

In this video from our FREE 9-Part Freight Broker Training Series, we explain the difference between the BMC-84 surety bond and BMC-85 trust fund, and why understanding these requirements is important before opening a freight brokerage in the USA.

🎓 WATCH THE COMPLETE FREE 9-PART FREIGHT BROKER TRAINING SERIES:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL4E4WjVdxrOcsOThu5qjzF6Pi8ep3kCI_

📋 WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:

✅ 1. WHAT IS THE $75,000 FREIGHT BROKER BOND REQUIREMENT?

US property brokers must maintain qualifying financial security of $75,000 under FMCSA requirements.

This financial security helps protect eligible parties when a freight broker fails to meet certain payment obligations.

✅ 2. BMC-84 SURETY BOND

A BMC-84 is a surety bond issued by an authorized surety provider.

Instead of depositing the full $75,000, brokers generally pay a premium based on factors such as creditworthiness, financial history, and underwriting requirements.

The premium is not the same as the bond's $75,000 penal sum.

✅ 3. BMC-85 TRUST FUND

A BMC-85 is an alternative financial security arrangement established through an eligible financial institution.

It requires $75,000 in qualifying security, subject to applicable FMCSA rules and provider requirements.

Unlike a surety bond premium, this arrangement can tie up a substantial amount of capital.

✅ 4. BMC-84 VS. BMC-85 — WHICH SHOULD YOU CHOOSE?

Important factors to consider include:

• Initial cash requirements

• Annual bond premiums or trust administration costs

• Credit and underwriting qualifications

• Financial security obligations

• Provider eligibility and compliance

• Available startup capital

✅ 5. HOW DOES FMCSA VERIFY YOUR FINANCIAL SECURITY?

The required BMC-84 or BMC-85 filing must be submitted through the appropriate process before broker operating authority can become active.

🚛 IMPORTANT FOR NEW FREIGHT BROKERS

You do not necessarily need to deposit $75,000 in cash when using a qualifying BMC-84 surety bond.

However, the broker remains responsible for its obligations, and a surety bond is not the same as insurance that eliminates liability for unpaid freight bills.

🎓 FREE 9-PART FREIGHT BROKER TRAINING SERIES

Learn how to start a freight broker business, including:

• Freight broker earning potential

• FMCSA broker authority

• The $75,000 freight broker bond

• LLC vs. Corporation

• Setting up a freight broker office

• Load boards and freight broker software

• Finding shippers and customers

• Moving your first freight load

👇 WATCH ALL 9 EPISODES FREE:
https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PL4E4WjVdxrOcsOThu5qjzF6Pi8ep3kCI_

🚛 WANT MORE IN-DEPTH FREIGHT BROKER TRAINING?

Freight Broker Training Course:
https://truckingacademy.us/products/freight-broker-training-course

⚠️ This video is educational. FMCSA financial security requirements, provider eligibility, and bond or trust terms can change. Verify current requirements with FMCSA and qualified financial security providers. US FMCSA authority does not automatically satisfy separate Canadian regulatory requirements.

metadata.title: Defining FMCSA Operating Authority Types for Freight Forwarders and Brokers (FMCSA OFFICIAL VIDEO)
metadata.author: FMCSA
metadata.shortDescription: Continuing with the FMCSA’s Office of Registration “HOW TO” Video Series, we would like to present “HOW TO Define FMCSA Operating Authority (OA) Types for Freight Forwarders and Brokers”.  If you’re registering with FMCSA for the first time, or if you are expanding your operations to offer additional services, you need to understand the requirements for Operating Authority (OA).  In this video, we cover the types of Operating Authority (OA) for Brokers and Freight Forwarders, as these are distinct and different from Motor Carrier of Property (except Household Goods), Motor Carrier of Household Goods, and Motor Carrier of Passengers.  The video summarizes regulatory guidance FMCSA issued on June 16, 2023, clarifying the definitions of “broker” and “bona fide agents”.  It also explains the minimum levels of financial responsibility in the form of either a surety bond or trust fund agreement for $75,000 that both brokers and freight forwarders must maintain, as well as the appropriate levels of bodily injury and property damage insurance freight forwarders must maintain if they operate commercial motor vehicles.  In addition, brokers and freight forwarders must designate a Process Agent in each State that they operate.

under

must have
either a surety bond filed by an insurance company
Or a trust fund agreement

All insurance companies and financial institutions must be approved
by FMCSA and submit these electronic filings with FMCSA.
FMCSA
requires both Brokers and Freight
Forwarders to designate a Process Agent.
Freight Forwarders that operate commercial
vehicles must designate a Process Agent in each state they
operate in or through.
You must have a BOC-3 form on file submitted

commercial vehicles must designate a Process Agent in each state in which

metadata.title: Truckstop Load Board Tutorial: Find the Loads DAT Misses in 2026
metadata.author: Dispatch Desk USA
metadata.shortDescription:
A truck sat empty in Dallas. DAT showed nothing worth calling on — then one filter change on Truckstop found a flatbed load picking up the next morning, forty miles from the truck. This video is the full Truckstop walkthrough. What Truckstop is: started in 1995 as Internet Truckstop, today the second-largest digital freight marketplace in North America — and how it differs from DAT (Book It Now instant booking, broker ratings and days-to-pay data, strongest in flatbed and open-deck, cheaper entry; DAT still wins on raw van and reefer volume — see Video #2). Step 1 — set up the search: origin and pickup radius, destination, equipment type, pickup date, plus advanced filters (minimum rate per mile, maximum deadhead, weight, length, broker authority age) and truck posting. Step 2 — read a posting line by line: pickup/delivery, miles, weight, broker, Book It Now badge, posting age, and the comments where the real cost hides. Step 3 — check the rate: Rate Insights (formerly Rate Mate, Pro plan) for the lane average, range, and trend — and the Video #20 rule, rate per ALL miles: the worked example on screen is $1,600 for 400 loaded miles ($4.00 per loaded mile) with 100 deadhead miles = $3.20 per all miles (example only, not a real load). Step 4 — book it: Book It Now (one click, fixed rate, Advanced plan and up) vs calling the broker, with the exact words to say on the call — and get the rate confirmation in writing before the truck moves (Video #24). Step 5 — red flags: too-good rates, vague postings, and the thirty-second broker check (factorability, ratings, days-to-pay, FMCSA SAFER authority check — Video #16). Plans at the time of this recording: Basic $42, Advanced $135, Pro $159 per user per month, plus a $42 application fee credited to the first month if approved — check Truckstop's site for current prices. No real carrier, broker, MC/DOT number, load number, lane, or address anywhere in this video. The formula: search tight, read the posting, check the rate, check the broker, book it right.

metadata.title: How Freight Factoring Helps Carriers Improve Cash Flow
metadata.author: BLACK BEAR FREIGHT & LOGISTICS
metadata.shortDescription:
You delivered the load and submitted the invoice—but the broker may not pay for another 30, 45, or even 60 days. Meanwhile, fuel, insurance, payroll, maintenance, and truck payments are due now.

In this video, we explain how freight factoring helps carriers convert unpaid freight invoices into working capital—and what you should examine before signing a factoring agreement.

You’ll learn:
- How freight factoring works
- Why cash flow and profit are not the same
- Recourse versus non-recourse factoring
- Why a low advertised rate may not represent the total cost
- Customer approval and concentration limits
- Notice of Assignment and payment control
- UCC filings and contract-exit considerations
- When factoring makes sense
- How factoring compares with quick pay and cash reserves
Freight factoring can help stabilize cash flow, support growth, and keep trucks moving. However, it cannot repair unprofitable rates or poor cost control. Use it as a financial tool—not as a substitute for a profitable operation.

Need help organizing your loads, documentation, billing, or carrier operation?

Contact Black Bear Freight & Logistics
🌐 BlackBearFreight.com

If this video helped you, give it a like, subscribe, and follow us for practical content about trucking, dispatch, freight management, cash flow, and business operations.

Disclaimer: This video is for general educational purposes and does not constitute financial or legal advice. Factoring rates, terms, protections, and requirements vary by company and agreement. Review the complete contract before signing.

segments.text: You delivered the load, submitted the
pod, and sent the invoice.
Great.
The work is finished. Well,
almost.
The broker or shipper may not pay for
30, 45, or even 60 days, but your fuel
card, insurance company, driver, truck
payment, and repair shop are definitely
not waiting 60 days.
And that gap between completing the load
and actually receiving the money is
where freight factoring can become
useful. Today, we'll explain how freight
factoring works,
what it really costs, the difference
between recourse and non-recourse
factoring, and several details carriers
often overlook before signing an
agreement.
And if you enjoy practical trucking
business content without the financial
fairy tales, give this video a like and
follow or subscribe to Black Bear
Freight and Logistics. Let's get
started.
Freight factoring is not a traditional
business loan. Instead, a carrier sells
an eligible freight invoice to a
factoring company.
The factor advances most of the invoice
value, sometimes on the same day or
within 24 hours, and later collects
payment from the broker or shipper.
For example, imagine that you deliver a
load worth $3,000.
Instead of waiting 40 days, the
factoring company may advance the money
quickly minus its fee or according to
the agreement's advanced structure.
That immediate cash can then cover fuel,
payroll, insurance, maintenance,
permits, and the next load.
The main benefit is simple. Factoring
converts accounts receivable into
working cash, but convenience always has
a price, so the details matter.
This is an important distinction. A
carrier can be profitable on paper and
still run out of cash.
Suppose your business earns more revenue
than it spends during the month. That
sounds healthy.
However,
however, if customers have not paid
those invoices yet, the money exists
only in accounts receivable.
Meanwhile, your operating expenses are
due now.
Profit measures whether the business is
economically sustainable. Cash flow
measures whether the business can pay
its obligations when they arrive.
Factoring does not automatically make an
unprofitable carrier profitable. It
simply accelerates access to money the
carrier has already earned.
If your rates are too low or your costs
are too high, getting paid faster will
not solve the underlying problem. It may
only help you lose money more
efficiently, which is impressive but not
the goal.
One of the most misunderstood parts of
factoring is the difference between
recourse and non-recourse agreements.
With recourse factoring, the carrier
generally remains responsible if the
customer does not pay after a specified
period. The factor may charge the
invoice back, deduct it from a reserve,
or replace it with another invoice.
Recourse factoring is often less
expensive because the carrier retains
more of the payment risk. With
non-recourse factoring, the factor may
accept certain credit risks, but this
protection is rarely unlimited.
Many non-recourse agreements only
protect against a defined event, such as
an approved customer becoming insolvent.
They may not protect the carrier if the
invoice is disputed, the POD is missing,
the load has a claim, the rate
confirmation does not match, or the
broker simply refuses payment for a
reason excluded by the contract.
So non-recourse does not necessarily
mean you can never be charged back. Read
the exclusions.
That section is usually more important
than the headline.
A low advertised rate can be attractive,
but the factoring percentage may not
represent the total cost.
Ask about ACH or wire transfer fees,
same-day funding charges, minimum
monthly volume requirements, invoice
processing fees, credit check fees,
reserve requirements, early termination
penalties, contract renewal provisions,
fees that increase as an invoice gets
older.
Some agreements use a flat fee, others
use a tiered structure in which the cost
increases every 10, 15, or 30 days until
the customer pays. That means the
broker's payment speed can directly
affect your final factoring cost.
Before signing, request a written
example showing the total cost of
factoring a typical invoice if it is
paid in 15,
30, 45, and 60 days.
That one question can reveal much more
than a promotional percentage.
Factoring companies usually evaluate the
broker or shipper, not only the carrier,
because that customer is expected to pay
the invoice. A factor may approve one
broker, assign a low credit limit to
another, and reject a third.
This can protect carriers from
financially weak customers, but factor
approval is not a guarantee that a load
is safe or profitable. You still need to
verify the broker, authority, payment
history, rate confirmation, and load
details. Carriers should also ask about
concentration limits.
If 40% of your invoices come from one
broker,
the factor may limit how much exposure
it will accept from that customer.
A carrier can have plenty of freight and
still face a funding problem because too
much revenue is concentrated in one
account.
That detail matters significantly for
dedicated lanes and recurring customers.
When an invoice is factored, the broker
or shipper normally receives a notice of
assignment.
This notice tells the customer that
payment must go directly to the
factoring company.
Once the notice is active, the carrier
should not casually ask the broker to
send payment somewhere else.
Misdirected payments can create
reconciliation problems, delays, and
possible contract violations. The factor
may also file a UCC financing statement
covering accounts receivable or related
business assets.
That is common, but carriers should
understand the scope of the filing
and how it will be released when the
relationship ends.
If you later want to change factoring
companies, an unresolved UCC filing or
unpaid termination balance can delay the
transition.
The exit process matters almost as much
as the sign-up process.
Factoring may be useful when a new
authority has limited working capital,
customers have reliable credit but slow
payment terms, the carrier is growing
faster than its available cash,
payroll and fuel must be paid before
invoices mature,
the carrier wants outsourced invoice
collection and payment tracking.
It may be less attractive when the
business has strong cash reserves,
customers pay quickly, or the total
factoring cost is higher than other
available financing options.
Some brokers also offer quick pay.
Compare its complete cost and payment
speed with factoring.
Quick pay may work for selected
invoices, while factoring may include
broader credit checking, collections,
fuel programs, and administrative
support.
The cheapest percentage is not always
the best solution.
Flexibility, service quality, contract
terms, and funding reliability also have
value.
Freight factoring can improve cash flow
by turning unpaid invoices into usable
working capital.
But remember, fast money is not free
money.
Understand the fee structure, recourse
provisions, customer limits, reserve
policies, UCC filing, termination terms,
and what happens when an invoice is
disputed.

videos.full_text: You delivered the load, submitted the pod, and sent the invoice. Great. The work is finished. Well, almost. The broker or shipper may not pay for 30, 45, or even 60 days, but your fuel card, insurance company, driver, truck payment, and repair shop are definitely not waiting 60 days. And that gap between completing the load and actually receiving the money is where freight factoring can become useful. Today, we'll explain how freight factoring works, what it really costs, the difference between recourse and non-recourse factoring, and several details carriers often overlook before signing an agreement. And if you enjoy practical trucking business content without the financial fairy tales, give this video a like and follow or subscribe to Black Bear Freight and Logistics. Let's get started. Freight factoring is not a traditional business loan. Instead, a carrier sells an eligible freight invoice to a factoring company. The factor advances most of the invoice value, sometimes on the same day or within 24 hours, and later collects payment from the broker or shipper. For example, imagine that you deliver a load worth $3,000. Instead of waiting 40 days, the factoring company may advance the money quickly minus its fee or according to the agreement's advanced structure. That immediate cash can then cover fuel, payroll, insurance, maintenance, permits, and the next load. The main benefit is simple. Factoring converts accounts receivable into working cash, but convenience always has a price, so the details matter. This is an important distinction. A carrier can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash. Suppose your business earns more revenue than it spends during the month. That sounds healthy. However, however, if customers have not paid those invoices yet, the money exists only in accounts receivable. Meanwhile, your operating expenses are due now. Profit measures whether the business is economically sustainable. Cash flow measures whether the business can pay its obligations when they arrive. Factoring does not automatically make an unprofitable carrier profitable. It simply accelerates access to money the carrier has already earned. If your rates are too low or your costs are too high, getting paid faster will not solve the underlying problem. It may only help you lose money more efficiently, which is impressive but not the goal. One of the most misunderstood parts of factoring is the difference between recourse and non-recourse agreements. With recourse factoring, the carrier generally remains responsible if the customer does not pay after a specified period. The factor may charge the invoice back, deduct it from a reserve, or replace it with another invoice. Recourse factoring is often less expensive because the carrier retains more of the payment risk. With non-recourse factoring, the factor may accept certain credit risks, but this protection is rarely unlimited. Many non-recourse agreements only protect against a defined event, such as an approved customer becoming insolvent. They may not protect the carrier if the invoice is disputed, the POD is missing, the load has a claim, the rate confirmation does not match, or the broker simply refuses payment for a reason excluded by the contract. So non-recourse does not necessarily mean you can never be charged back. Read the exclusions. That section is usually more important than the headline. A low advertised rate can be attractive, but the factoring percentage may not represent the total cost. Ask about ACH or wire transfer fees, same-day funding charges, minimum monthly volume requirements, invoice processing fees, credit check fees, reserve requirements, early termination penalties, contract renewal provisions, fees that increase as an invoice gets older. Some agreements use a flat fee, others use a tiered structure in which the cost increases every 10, 15, or 30 days until the customer pays. That means the broker's payment speed can directly affect your final factoring cost. Before signing, request a written example showing the total cost of factoring a typical invoice if it is paid in 15, 30, 45, and 60 days. That one question can reveal much more than a promotional percentage. Factoring companies usually evaluate the broker or shipper, not only the carrier, because that customer is expected to pay the invoice. A factor may approve one broker, assign a low credit limit to another, and reject a third. This can protect carriers from financially weak customers, but factor approval is not a guarantee that a load is safe or profitable. You still need to verify the broker, authority, payment history, rate confirmation, and load details. Carriers should also ask about concentration limits. If 40% of your invoices come from one broker, the factor may limit how much exposure it will accept from that customer. A carrier can have plenty of freight and still face a funding problem because too much revenue is concentrated in one account. That detail matters significantly for dedicated lanes and recurring customers. When an invoice is factored, the broker or shipper normally receives a notice of assignment. This notice tells the customer that payment must go directly to the factoring company. Once the notice is active, the carrier should not casually ask the broker to send payment somewhere else. Misdirected payments can create reconciliation problems, delays, and possible contract violations. The factor may also file a UCC financing statement covering accounts receivable or related business assets. That is common, but carriers should understand the scope of the filing and how it will be released when the relationship ends. If you later want to change factoring companies, an unresolved UCC filing or unpaid termination balance can delay the transition. The exit process matters almost as much as the sign-up process. Factoring may be useful when a new authority has limited working capital, customers have reliable credit but slow payment terms, the carrier is growing faster than its available cash, payroll and fuel must be paid before invoices mature, the carrier wants outsourced invoice collection and payment tracking. It may be less attractive when the business has strong cash reserves, customers pay quickly, or the total factoring cost is higher than other available financing options. Some brokers also offer quick pay. Compare its complete cost and payment speed with factoring. Quick pay may work for selected invoices, while factoring may include broader credit checking, collections, fuel programs, and administrative support. The cheapest percentage is not always the best solution. Flexibility, service quality, contract terms, and funding reliability also have value. Freight factoring can improve cash flow by turning unpaid invoices into usable working capital. But remember, fast money is not free money. Understand the fee structure, recourse provisions, customer limits, reserve policies, UCC filing, termination terms, and what happens when an invoice is disputed. Most importantly, use factoring as a cash flow tool, not as a substitute for profitable rates and disciplined cost management. If this video helped you understand factoring beyond the sales pitch, give it a like, subscribe, and follow Black Bear Freight and Logistics for more practical content about trucking, dispatch, freight management, and business operations. And if you need help organizing your loads, documentation, billing, or carrier operation, contact Black Bear Freight and Logistics. Drive safely, protect your cash flow, and we'll see you in the next video.
